news.title: Karine Jean-Pierre says Trump is making same mistake as Biden on fulfilling his agenda
news.text:
Former White House press secretary Karine Jean-Pierre argued in an opinion piece published Friday that President Donald Trump was making the same messaging mistakes as her former boss, former President Joe Biden.

“Mr. Biden wanted his team to highlight his domestic agenda,” she wrote in The New York Times guest essay. “His policies were working, and he wanted the country to understand what he was doing and why. But the polling was clear: Our economic message didn’t land. 

“Too many people were struggling with the prices of groceries, rent, child care and gas. Their lived experience did not match the encouraging economic news, and that disconnect shaped the entire public conversation.”

Jean-Pierre pointed to the president’s messaging on gas prices, inflation and the war in Iran in the piece and said, “When leaders neglect lived experience, the message collapses.”

“The truth is, we had a stale message and outdated models for delivering it. It cost Mr. Biden and, eventually, Vice President Kamala Harris dearly. President Trump is now making a mistake even more damaging,” she wrote.

When asked about Jean-Pierre’s argument, White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told Fox News Digital in a statement, “Biden’s policies destroyed our economy by creating the worst inflation crisis in history, instituting burdensome red tape and stifling American energy dominance. 

“President Trump has fixed the disaster that Joe Biden created by cooling inflation, signing the largest middle-class tax cuts in history, lowering drug prices and reshoring our manufacturing industry. The fake news won’t, so President Trump will continue to tout his economic wins to Americans.”

Jean-Pierre admitted the Biden administration misread the public and said her press briefings fueled much of the debate surrounding Biden’s age, in addition to the economic messaging.

“We learned that lesson with the economy and again with the debate around Mr. Biden’s age. Looking back, we misread the public mood, thinking the age conversation would fade. At best, my responses from the podium about Mr. Biden’s age failed to put out the fire; at worst, they fueled it,” she conceded.

She also pointed to the changing media ecosystem and said a “TikTok about high prices, filmed with a phone in a grocery store aisle or in front of a gas pump” would get more attention than her press briefings or a Cabinet official on the Sunday news programs.

“The Trump White House should realize that over the next two years, there will be only more, not less, scrutiny when the president appears to drift off during meetings, is cagey about the results of his medical exams or goes on one of his erratic, late-night social media screeds,” Jean-Pierre wrote. 

“His communications team should know by now that the prices at the pump and the self-checkout line are undefeated.

“Once people believe their government is not speaking to their reality, it becomes incredibly difficult to earn that trust back. I felt that tension every day in the White House briefing room. I see it happening again now.”

Jean-Pierre released a book in 2025, “Independent,” about her time in the White House. 

Ahead of its release, she revealed she was leaving the Democratic Party and registering as an Independent.

“The Democratic Party had defined my life, my career,” Jean-Pierre wrote. 

“Everything I’d done to make people’s lives better had been connected to it. The party was the vehicle that allowed me not just to have a front seat to history, working first on [Barack] Obama’s presidential campaign then in his administration, but also to make some history of my own as the first Black woman and openly queer person to ever be a White House press secretary. Never had I considered leaving the party until now.”
news.summary: In a New York Times essay, Karine Jean-Pierre warns that Donald Trump is repeating Joe Biden's mistake of ignoring voters' lived economic realities.

news.title: The good news on federal workers you probably never heard about
news.text:
One of the most unheralded policy successes of President Donald Trump’s second term has been the purging of many unnecessary federal jobs.

The federal government has reduced its workforce by 300,000 jobs since Jan. 20, 2025, bringing it down to a still-bulky 2.7 million employees.

Not since President Lyndon Johnson’s Great Society vastly expanded the scope of the national government has the federal workforce been at this level.

It’s not merely that the feds have shed superfluous jobs — there are still over 4 million contract workers, after all.

It’s that the White House has been targeting all the right institutions.

The bloated War Department, with over 61,000 departures, and the equally bloated State Department, with 37% of its staff gone, experienced the biggest reductions.

But most of the buyouts were aimed at agencies and departments that should have been shuttered a long time ago.

Take the US Agency for International Development, which for years was used to funnel billions to hard-left ideological projects around the world: Virtually its entire staff is gone.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the unaccountable bureaucratic brainchild of progressive Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), has lost roughly 88% of its workers, though it’s still far too big.

The Agriculture Department, which despite its name is principally a welfare agency that has little to do with farming, experienced tens of thousands of departures.

So has another welfare-state institution, the Department of Housing and Urban Development, whose most notable achievement has been helping inflate housing prices.

Not every agency is being clipped fast enough, though.

Early in his term, Trump signed an executive order directing the dismantling of the Education Department — yet this intrusive agency, which spends its time propping up unions and undermining local initiatives, has lost only 40% of its staff.

Every time Republicans threaten to cut federal jobs, though they rarely follow through, Democrats predict that society will be plunged into chaos and high unemployment.

The unemployment rate in September 2024 was 4.1%.

In September 2025, it was 4.4%.

It’s at 4.2% today.

Barely anyone, one suspects, has noticed that the federal workforce has shrunk by around 11%.

They probably wouldn’t notice if it shrank by another 11%.

What Democrats really fear is losing power.

Federal agencies, government employees and public-sector unions are all bases of political influence for the left.

“This is an attempt at intimidation,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) complained when the Office of Management and Budget released a memo instructing agencies to plan for large-scale layoffs.

“Donald Trump has been firing federal workers since Day 1 — not to govern, but to scare.”

Why would Democrats be “scared” of a leaner federal workforce?

We don’t know how government employees vote, but we can make an educated guess.

Around 84% of campaign donations from federal workers went to Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris in 2024.

Federal civilian jobs rose by over 130,000 under the Biden administration.

Around 11% of the approximately 16 million US jobs added during Biden’s term were federal, state and local government jobs.

Roughly 15% of the total US workforce, around 24 million people, still works for the government at all levels.

There is more that can be done, not only in trimming the federal workforce but also in decentralizing and dispersing it.

Trump promised to relocate more federal jobs out of the Washington area — the political class entrenched around the capital in Virginia and Maryland keeps voting to empower itself.

It should be dispersed as much as possible.

In 2001, anti-tax activist Grover Norquist famously proclaimed that his goal was to shrink the federal government until it was small enough to “drag it into the bathroom and drown it in the bathtub.”

We’ve learned over the years that it doesn’t work that way: Neither party has any plan to curb spending, and voters don’t seem to be clamoring for one.

Shrinking the federal bureaucracy and workforce isn’t going to restrain massive deficit spending and our economy-threatening, turbocharged debt.

Still, paring down the size, scope and intrusiveness of a swollen federal government, even if it’s just temporary until Democrats come back into power, is a win for taxpayers.

David Harsanyi is a senior writer at the Washington Examiner.
news.summary: The federal government has reduced its workforce by 300,000 jobs since Jan. 20, 2025, bringing it down to a still-bulky 2.7 million employees.

news.title: Dana Perino Scolds Jesse Watters for Spilling Fox News Secrets on Live TV: 'You Need to Get It Together'
news.text:

news.title: ‘Barbaric slaughter’: Report shows organ-harvesting company was paid $765 each for livers, glands from unborn killed
news.text:
A corporation that sold individual body parts from unborn babies killed by abortion, for $765 each, insists that its billing reflect that it was charging for “procurement services,” not actual taxable “items.”

“The fetal organ harvesting business murders innocent babies for profit. These public records obtained by the Center for Medical Progress show that the work must continue to expose these heinous acts by these abortionists, harvesters, researchers, universities, and companies. The barbaric slaughter of babies for profit must stop,” charged Mat Staver, the chief of Liberty Counsel.

His organization long has worked with the CMP, defending one of its original reporters, Sandra Merritt, from a multitude of cases brought by pro-abortion interests after the center revealed, through undercover videos, the abortion industry’s profit motive.

One abortionist talked, on video, about raising the price of baby body parts being delivered mostly to researchers because “I want a Lamborghini.”

CMP now has obtained public records showing the fetal organ-harvesting corporation called Cercle Allocation Services billed a UCLA research lab $765 for each body part.

“Peer-reviewed research confirms that Cercle, which has previously harvested organs under the name Advanced Bioscience Research, has been a source of human fetal tissue for researchers. ABR and its partners at Planned Parenthood were the subject of congressional criminal referrals in 2016 prompted by CMP’s undercover video reporting in 2015 by David Daleiden and Sandra Merritt who exposed Planned Parenthood’s aborted baby body parts trade,” Liberty Counsel reported.

The legal team defended Merritt against felony charges and in a civil suit for uncovering the truth about the abortion giant’s horrific trade in baby body parts.

The report said CMP got the documents through a California Public Records request, and they show “purchase orders and email correspondence between Cercle and UCLA’s David Geffen School of Medicine’s Division of Hematology-Oncology.”

There was a total of $16,065 paid to Cercle in 2023 for 21 body parts of aborted infants.

“Federal law makes it a felony to ‘knowingly acquire, receive, or otherwise transfer any human fetal tissue for valuable consideration if the transfer affects interstate commerce,'” the report said.

And emails confirm Cercle officials worried about the billing.

“The overriding issue is the use of terminology that we must not use due to their improper implication that we are selling taxable items, which we are not,” stated a Cercle account manager in an email September 2023. “Due to the nature of our business, we must be very careful and clear that we invoice fees for our procurement services (untaxable).”

Liberty Counsel reported, “The records also indicate that ABR has sold FDA-regulated fetal organs for up to $7,000 each, and that Cercle had to cancel a March 2025 order for a fetal brain because it could not be obtained.”

Also revealed along with the records was evidence of a “financial incentive,” which CMP addressed in a documentary called, “What Happened to Clementine.”

Daleiden said, “These new records from Cercle’s abortion side business harvesting baby body parts show the extreme financial incentives that exist for ‘research’ abortions to deliver whole, preemie-size babies alive—as appears to have been done to baby Clementine and her mother, and potentially thousands of others.”

After CMP revealed the apparent body parts deals in a series of undercover videos, California authorities retaliated.

“California state prosecutors—beginning with then-Attorney General Kamala Harris and continuing with Xavier Becerra, now a California gubernatorial candidate—pursued nine years of litigation against Daleiden and Merritt alleging illegal secret recordings,” Liberty Counsel confirmed.

“In January 2025, the state of California agreed to end its prosecution of the two journalists. Liberty Counsel negotiated on behalf of Merritt where the state Attorney General’s office agreed to end the case against her with no prison time, no fines, and only a ‘No Contest’ pleading to one felony charge, which was reduced to a misdemeanor after a one-year probationary period and then expunged from her record entirely. Daleiden received the same settlement agreement, which was essentially a complete victory for both journalists in a politically motivated criminal case.”
news.summary: Officials insisted billing was for 'procurement services,' not actual 'taxable items'
news.author: Bob Unruh

news.title: Colbert Writers Find New Home With His Late-Night Competitor
news.text:
Stephen Colbert’s former Late Show staffers are returning to late-night. 

Months after Paramount axed Colbert’s show, Late Show writers Ariel Dumas and Asher Perlman have found homes on The Tonight Show with Jimmy Fallon, according to LateNighter. 

Perlman, a contributing cartoonist for The New Yorker, joined The Late Show staff in 2019, following his tenure on Comedy Central’s The Opposition with Jordan Klepper. He hosts the Jokes on News podcast with his former Late Show colleagues Steve Waltien, Eliana Kwartler, Michael Cruz and Kayne.

Both Dumas and Perlman made on-camera appearances on The Late Show before the show aired its last episode on May 21. 

The show’s cancellation came after years of back-and-forth with Donald Trump, and Colbert’s declaring on air that his network’s parent company, Paramount, “bribed” the president with its $16.6 million payout to settle his lawsuit over Kamala Harris’ 60 Minutes interview. 

Paramount needed approval from Trump’s administration to merge with Skydance at the time, but the network declared that axing Colbert and The Late Show franchise were “purely financial” decisions. 

Colbert’s former staff have been defiant, accusing the company of leaving them in the lurch for Emmy nominations, though the team ultimately won Outstanding Writing for a Variety Series and Outstanding Variety Series for The Late Show’s last season.

LateNighter reports that Dumas has been hired as The Tonight Show’s sketch writing supervisor. She told Vanity Fair that the job started just days after the Emmys. As for how it’s going, she told the publication, “I’m only on day three, so at this point, I’m just still trying to remember which floor the cafeteria is on.”

Both comedians are stepping into markedly different territory from Colbert’s fiery anti-Trump show as they join Fallon’s team. When Jimmy Kimmel was suspended from ABC after angering MAGA, following threats from Trump’s FCC, Fallon told CNBC he was “keeping his head down.”

“Our show’s never really been that political,” he said last September. “We hit both sides equally, and we try to make everybody laugh.”
news.summary:

Months after Paramount axed Colbert’s show, Late Show writers Ariel Dumas and Asher Perlman have found homes on The Tonight Show with Jimmy Fallon, according to LateNighter. 

Dumas, the show’s head writer, led the team of fired writers when Emmy host Mariska Hargitay hired them to write for this year’s awards show. She worked for Colbert on The Colbert Report and followed the host when he took over The Late Show from David Letterman on CBS in 2015.

news.title: Why Is Local Media Running Cover for Janelle Stelson in PA-10?
news.text:
Democrat Janelle Stelson is running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 10th District. Like most Democrats, she's telling voters one thing while telling her fellow Democrats in D.C. another thing.

One of those issues is illegal immigration. On October 8, 2024, Stelson told local media, "We also need to send people who cross illegally or are here illegally. We need to send them home." Less than a month later, Stelson told D.C. Democrats that she wanted illegal aliens to be "assimilated into our communities and neighborhoods" to "get them ... working, sending money back home, which is what many of them dream of doing."

A few weeks ago, the Congressional Leadership Fund (CLF) dropped an ad highlighting Stelson's views on illegal immigration, including allowing taxpayer benefits to pay for illegal aliens while supporting a plan to close rural hospitals in Pennsylvania.

Ian Thompson, a story desk editor at Fox 43/WPMT, the Harrisburg/Lebanon/Lancaster/York Fox affiliate, reached out to CLF to ask them for their source on the information in their Stelson ad.

The source was Thompson's own station, particularly this interview with Stelson, where Stelson says around the 11 minute mark that she supports a "pathway to citizenship for dreamers," among other things.

CLF says it provided the answer to Thompson, but he kept pestering them. It turns out Thompson is a left-wing partisan who hates President Trump and has written extensively about his political views, as recently as 2024.

In a 2024 opinion piece for The Slate, the student newspaper for Shippensburg University, Thompson wrote:

I have made my views on Trump expressly clear — he is a wannabe-fascist who does not care for the rule of law, political institutions, or anybody but himself. He is a power-hungry aspiring tyrant.

Thompson and The Slate later endorsed Kamala Harris for president, and he wrote a defense of that piece, which is very telling:

As journalists, we have a duty to speak the truth. The truth is Trump is a danger to the country he wants to run, in his own words, as a dictator. The truth is that Trump is unfit to be president, and we have a duty to make that fact known.

And Thompson also criticized the tens of millions of Americans who are Trump voters:

I feel sorry for these people. I don't know what it is — cognitive dissonance, sunk cost fallacy, obstinance. In the face of tangible, material harm to their livelihoods and security, it is depressing that so many Americans still cling to such blind loyalty and faith to a man who has demonstrated in every possible way that he has always been a con man.

Therefore, it's no surprise that Ian Thompson covered for Stelson in a recent fact check about CLF's ads. But as we noted, the source for some of the CLF's ads is Thompson's own station.

Stelson herself was a journalist, and Thompson — who has made no secret of his anti-Trump views — is covering for her.

"Janelle Stelson is a far-left progressive who masqueraded as a reporter for years," said CLF spokeswoman Lydia Hall. "Now that she can’t spin the news herself, her liberal reporter friends are covering for her. It’s deceitful and wrong. Here’s the real story: Stelson is a far-left radical who will make Pennsylvania even less affordable with socialist programs and benefits for illegals."

news.title: Trump Energy Policies Could Add $6,500 to US Household Bills as Red States Face Bigger Hits
news.text: US households could face an additional $6,500 (£4,920) in cumulative energy costs through 2040 under federal energy-policy changes made since Donald Trump returned to office, with households in states he won in 2024 projected to face a larger average increase.The modelling puts the average additional cost at about $7,000 (£5,298) per household in Trump-voting states, compared with $5,800 (£4,390) in states won by Kamala Harris. The figures cover the 48 contiguous states and represent projected spending over 2026 to 2040, rather than an annual increase in electricity bills.That distinction matters because the projected hit extends beyond household electricity. The analysis incorporates both power and transport costs, including the effect of policies affecting vehicle efficiency and the development of new energy supplies.Red-State Exposure Is Not UniformThe state-level picture is more complicated than a simple Republican-versus-Democrat divide. Oregon, Mississippi, South Dakota, Virginia, and Wyoming are projected to record the largest cumulative household increases, at roughly $9,000 (£6,812) or more through 2040. Oregon is projected to see the biggest increase, at about $9,300 (£7,039) per household.Three of those five states have Republican governors, showing that the projected financial impact does not map neatly on to party control at state level. The broader Energy Innovation model estimates that federal policy decisions could add $920B (£696B) to household energy spending across the 48 states between 2026 and 2040. It also projects an average additional household cost of $640 (£484) in 2035 alone.Transport Costs Could Become a Bigger Part of the BillThe projected increase is not simply about what appears on an electricity statement. Energy Innovation estimates that changes affecting vehicle efficiency and transport-sector innovation could push petrol prices 54 cents (41p) per gallon higher in 2035 and 93 cents (70p) higher in 2040, compared with the policy baseline used in its modelling.That creates a second route through which energy policy could affect household budgets. Drivers could face higher fuel costs while households also absorb changes in electricity and heating expenses.The modelling incorporates the effect of the Iran war on energy-price forecasts but says it did not explicitly model individual tariffs. It also describes its household-cost assessment as conservative because some inflationary and technology-price effects are incorporated only where underlying data captures them.Electricity Prices Are Already RisingThe projections arrive as US residential electricity prices are already increasing. The latest US Energy Information Administration data shows the average residential electricity price reached 18.31 cents (14p) per kilowatt-hour in July 2026, up 4.9% from 17.45 cents (13p) a year earlier.The new modelling therefore addresses a wider affordability question: whether changes to the US energy mix and transport system could add to costs that households are already experiencing. Energy Innovation also estimates the policy changes could produce $72B (£54.5B) in additional healthcare costs and 37,000 premature deaths from increased air pollution through 2040. Those are modelled impacts, not current recorded household expenses.White House Disputes the Affordability OutlookThe Trump administration has argued that its energy strategy should reduce rather than increase household costs. The White House says expanding domestic energy production, protecting existing generation, and accelerating new power infrastructure will improve reliability and affordability.Its March 2026 Ratepayer Protection Pledge also requires participating technology companies to cover new power-generation and infrastructure costs associated with their data centres, rather than passing those costs on to households. The Energy Innovation modelling, however, assesses a different set of federal policy changes, including the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, environmental-rule changes, restrictions affecting renewable projects, and measures affecting vehicle emissions and efficiency.The result is a significant gap between the administration's stated affordability goals and the model's projected household costs. For consumers, the key figure is not a guaranteed future bill, but the estimated cumulative effect of policy choices on the cost of powering homes and fuelling vehicles through 2040.

news.title: Annie Andrews Polling Against Graham Compared to Harrison in 2020
news.text: Democrat Annie Andrews trailed Republican Senator Darline Graham by only a single point in a new poll of the South Carolina Senate race published on Friday, as Democrats eye the Palmetto state as a potential pickup opportunity in the 2026 midterm elections. South Carolina has long been one of the most solidly conservative states in the country, backing President Donald Trump by nearly 18 points in the 2024 presidential election. But as Trump’s nationwide approval rating slips, Democrats are hoping to expand the Senate map in the November 3 election. More traditionally Republican states like South Carolina, Kansas and Mississippi are drawing attention from Democrats in addition to double-digit Trump 2024 states that were already Senate battlegrounds like Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas. Graham was appointed to the Senate seat following the death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, and she won the party's nomination in the Senate race with the endorsement of Trump. Within the margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points, her support stood at 46 percent, while 45 percent said they planned to vote for Andrews, a doctor and former congressional candidate, in the new InsiderAdvantage poll of 1,200 likely voters. Other candidates received 5 percent support, while 4 percent were undecided, according to the poll, which was conducted from September 28 to 29, 2026. It’s the latest poll to show a close race in South Carolina. But South Carolina polls have disappointed Democrats in the past, including in 2020, when data showed a close race between Senator Lindsey Graham and Democrat Jaime Harrison, only for Graham to win reelection by 10 points. Newsweek reached out to the Andrews and Graham campaigns for comment via email. Darline Graham’s Narrow Lead in South Carolina Other polling has given Graham only a slight lead in South Carolina. A recent poll from Trafalgar Group, a Republican pollster, also showed her with a single-point lead, 43 percent to 42 percent, which falls within its margin of error of 2.9 points. It surveyed 1,087 likely voters from September 23 to 25. An earlier poll from InsiderAdvantage, conducted among 1,200 likely voters from September 8 to 9, showed Graham up only 2 points, 45 percent to 43 percent, which was also within the margin of error of 2.83 points. These polls mark a leftward shift from 2024, when Trump received 58 percent of the vote in South Carolina against former Vice President Kamala Harris’ 40 percent, an easy victory for the Republican president. But Democrats see national polls moving in their direction. A recent survey from YouGov and The Economist found that Democrats have a 15-point advantage on the generic ballot, 53 percent to 38 percent, among likely voters. It surveyed 1,003 likely voters from September 25 to 28. Trump’s approval rating has slipped nationwide amid ongoing frustration with the economy and the cost of living. Democrats believe these numbers could allow them to expand the battleground into more conservative territory like South Carolina. How Annie Andrews’ Polling Compares to Jaime Harrison Polling similarly showed a close race between Harrison and Graham in 2020. Of course, polling errors don't repeat from cycle to cycle, so it’s unclear whether there will be a miss this year, or which party could benefit. A Data for Progress poll released just days before the 2020 election showed Graham up only 3 points against Harrison, 49 percent to 46 percent. It surveyed 880 likely voters from October 27 to November 1, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.3 percentage points. Graham was up 2 points, 46 percent to 44 percent, in a poll from Morning Consult, which surveyed 904 likely voters from October 22 to 31, 2020, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. Can Annie Andrews Turn South Carolina Blue? While polls point to a closer race than expected, South Carolina is still a difficult state for Democrats. At the presidential level, South Carolina last voted for a Democratic candidate—former President Jimmy Carter—in 1976 and has given Republicans double-digit victories in recent cycles. Trump won by 18 points in 2024, nearly 12 points in 2020 and 14 points in 2016. The state backed Mitt Romney by 10 points in 2012 and John McCain by 9 points in 2008. South Carolina last elected a Democratic senator in 1998, when it sent Ernest Hollings to Congress’ upper chamber. South Carolina Democrats generally have a high floor but low ceiling. The Palmetto State is home to a high population of Black voters, who lean toward Democrats, and cities like Charleston and Columbia are more friendly to Democrats. But the more rural areas and suburbs, as well as a high level of racial polarization, have continued to give an advantage to the GOP. Still, Democrats believe the national environment may be challenging enough for Republicans to allow them to compete in more conservative states. Trump’s approval was underwater, according to Civiqs, which tracks his approval in each state. Fifty percent of South Carolina voters disapprove of him, while 44 percent give him positive marks, according to the pollster. What Happens Next Forecasters still give Graham an advantage in this race. The Cook Political Report classifies it as Likely Republican, while Sabato’s Crystal Ball views it as Safe Republican. Polls will continue to be watched as a key gauge of the electorate’s mood ahead of the midterms. news.summary: Darline Graham held a razor-thin lead over Annie Andrews in a new poll of the South Carolina Senate race.

news.title: Alabama Democrats see Trump’s Mobile rally as a sign of GOP nerves
news.text:
When President Donald Trump announced plans to campaign in Mobile for Alabama’s Republican statewide and congressional candidates, former Sen. Doug Jones figured the president was “trolling him.”

“We were coming to Mobile regardless of the fact that Donald Trump announced he was coming,” Jones, the Democratic nominee for governor, told a crowded room of students at an Auburn University voting event organized by the Alabama NAACP. “He sees what we're doing in this state, and he's like, ‘Oh Lord, I need to go down there and try to help somebody out.’”

Jones and other Alabama Democrats see Friday’s GOP rally as serving two purposes. It’s a chance for Trump to stroke his ego by returning to a state where he held one of the first major rallies in the 2016 campaign. And it’s an effort to fire up Republican voters who, Democrats argue, won’t turn out as eagerly as they did in 2024, when Trump carried the state by 30 points.

“Look, he can’t possibly think — given the numbers that we’re seeing in Alabama — that coming to Alabama actually helps,” Jones later told MS NOW. “I don’t think it hurts, but it doesn’t help, and so I just think it’s a distraction for everybody.”

The numbers Jones and other Democrats cite start with the cost of living: In a survey taken during this year’s primary season, 80% of Republican voters named it as their top issue. Democratic primary ballots nearly doubled between 2022 and 2026 — suggesting voter enthusiasm — while Republican ballots declined by more than 20%. And despite a redistricting push designed to make the 2nd Congressional District more favorable to Republicans, a Democratic Super PAC is saying it’s a close race. House Majority PAC has publicized limited results from a poll it commissioned that suggests the race between Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures and his Trump-backed Republican challenger, Rhett Marques, is basically tied.

Figures, whose current district includes Mobile, also sees Trump’s visit as a sign of Republican concern.

“He is attempting to go somewhere where he thinks he will be well received ahead of the midterm election, but I don’t know that to be the case necessarily in Alabama anymore when you look at the issues that people have with fuel prices; when you look at the impact that the tariffs have had with farmers,” Figures told MS NOW during a phone interview Thursday.

Jones, a former U.S. attorney, knows what’s possible when the political stars align. In 2017, during Trump’s first term and with the president’s approval ratings low, Jones won a Senate special election against Republican Roy Moore, who faced allegations of sexual misconduct.

But Jones has also felt the hard math facing Democrats in Alabama. In 2020, he lost his re-election bid by more than 20 points to Tommy Tuberville, the Trump-backed former Auburn football coach, in a year when Democrats won the White House and both chambers of Congress.

Now, six years later, Jones is back at the top of the Democratic ticket, betting that the conditions that produced his 2017 win can repeat themselves in November. He said he was spurred to run by a worsening affordability crisis under an unpopular Trump administration. And he faces a familiar opponent in Tuberville, who is running for governor rather than seeking re-election to the Senate and whose string of gaffes has unsettled some Republicans. Last month, Tuberville told CNN that Alabama voters were willing to withstand high fuel prices in support of Trump’s agenda.

As in much of the Deep South, a win by Jones or Figures hinges on mobilizing Black voters, who make up roughly a quarter of the state’s electorate. When Jones won in 2017, exit polls suggested Black voters turned out in higher numbers than white voters: They comprised roughly 30% of the overall electorate, a high-water mark that hasn’t been matched since.

Jones has little doubt that Black Alabamians will turn out in record numbers again.

“People have woken up to a lot of things, including the fact that Donald Trump has taken away their voting rights,” Jones said. “We saw the Alabama legislature go in and redistrict within 48 hours after that [Supreme Court] Callais decision that came through. People are upset about that, so I think there’s a newfound sense of urgency.”

The modern voting rights movement was forged in Alabama. The brutal repression of Black activists in Selma on what became known as “Bloody Sunday” helped spur Congress to pass the Voting Rights Act of 1965. The landmark law sought to dismantle racial discrimination in voting and expand Black political participation and representation.

For decades, Section 2 of the law was a principal safeguard against vote dilution: drawing district lines in ways that weaken minority voters’ ability to elect their preferred candidates.

In 2023, a federal court relied on Section 2 to impose a new congressional map in Alabama, creating a second district in which Black voters had a realistic chance to elect their preferred candidate. The court found that the state’s previous map had unlawfully diluted Black Alabamians’ voting power by concentrating much of the Black Belt in a single district. The result was historic: In 2024, Alabama’s congressional delegation included two Black members for the first time.

But the Supreme Court’s conservative majority sharply narrowed Section 2 in Louisiana v. Callais, making it harder for voters to challenge district lines they say dilute minority voting power. The ruling cleared the way for Alabama Republicans to adopt a map that a federal court had previously rejected, one that makes the 2nd District friendlier to the GOP by reducing its Black voting-age population.

Figures said voters in his district, which includes Montgomery, won’t quietly accept efforts to weaken their political voice.

“The civil rights history there is something that resonates in a unique way and it’s something that’s motivating people,” Figures told MS NOW. “I think we’ve seen this in primary turnout. In the Democratic-leaning counties of the district, we saw turnout increase almost over 20% in some counties compared to 2022.”

Still, Figures faces an uphill climb. Under the new lines, the district’s Black voting-age population drops from 48% to 40%, according to census data. That may not sound like much, but it produces a far more Republican-friendly electorate: Kamala Harris would have carried the old district by eight points, while Trump would have won the new one by double digits.

For now, at least, Figures has the edge on the airwaves. He has outspent Marques on advertising by more than $500,000, according to AdImpact.

Jones and Figures told MS NOW they are also courting other voters put off by Trump’s policies: cattle farmers angry about the loosening of tariffs on imported beef; Republicans increasingly frustrated by the war with Iran and its effect on fuel prices; and younger voters uneasy about the rapid spread of data centers, an issue several Auburn students raised in interviews on campus. Jones has called for a moratorium on new data centers. Tuberville has described them as “game changers” for communities across the state.

“As a person whose major revolves around creativity, I’m extremely opposed to the use of AI in a generative sense. But it also tears apart communities — rural communities like one that I am, I grew up in,” said Barrett Wilson, a 21-year-old Auburn senior who plans to back Jones.

Some students also saw Trump’s visit as an attempt to shore up support among frustrated Republicans.

“I’ve heard from the [Auburn College Republicans] president here. He also told me the same things that I’m telling you: that we don’t want to fight unnecessary wars that raise our prices,” Itamar Sorek, 19, told MS NOW. “This is not America First policy. We’ve seen the corruption firsthand. I think we’re all just tired of it.”

The coalition Jones aims to build reflects his belief that the midterms will not be a “blue wave” so much as a “change wave.”

“I think you’re seeing it play out around the country,” Jones said. “This is a change wave. People are fed up with both political parties, and they’re looking for change. And that’s what I think you’re seeing playing out, and it'll play out in Alabama.”

Trump’s Mobile rally is part of a multistate campaign swing that took him to Denton, Texas and Durant, Oklahoma, on Thursday and continues Saturday in Vandalia, Ohio. In Mobile, Tuberville is expected to introduce the president, and Marques is also set to speak, according to local reports.

Ronald Ali, chair of the Alabama NAACP, sees the president’s return to Mobile as both a nod to the past and a call to action.

“He started in Mobile when he began his journey. He’s coming to Mobile to try and continue his journey in terms of the influence that he represents,” Ali said. “My reaction would be, he has every right to do so, and I got every right to make sure I get out the vote.”

According to the survey, Talarico has done a much better job of acquiring the backing of self-described Democrats than Paxton has for Republicans. Overall, 99 percent of Democrats said they would back Talarico versus just 1 percent for Paxton. By contrast, only 90 percent of Republicans said they would vote for Paxton, with 10 percent opting for Talarico. Paxton’s difficulty was particularly pronounced with Republicans who don’t identify as MAGA, of whom 22 percent said they would vote for Talarico. By contrast, the poll showed he had the backing of 96 percent of MAGA Republicans, with only 4 percent going to Talarico. Notably, the poll found 37 percent of voters were “extremely concerned,” and another 14 percent were “very concerned” that Paxton “is too close to Donald Trump. By contrast, 29 percent of respondents said they were “not at all concerned,” while another 20 percent answered, “not very concerned.” Overall, once rounding was taken into account, 51 percent were “extremely” or “very” concerned, while 48 percent were “not very” or “not at all” concerned and another 1 percent answered, “don’t know.” Even among voters who identified as “non-MAGA” Republicans, 39 percent were “extremely” or “very” concerned about Paxton’s relationship with Trump, while 61 percent were “not very” or “not at all” bothered. By contrast, among voters identifying as “MAGA” Republicans, only 10 percent were “extremely” or “very” concerned, while 89 percent were “not at all” or “not very” concerned. The survey also found 63 percent of Texan voters said Trump would be “extremely” or “very” important for their Senate vote, against 36 percent for “not very” or “not at all” important. This matches the result of a Big Data Poll of 698 likely Texas voters conducted between September 24 and 26, which found Talarico had the support of 15 percent of 2024 Trump voters, while Paxton only had the backing of 4.2 percent of 2024 Kamala Harris voters. Trump Rally During his speech in Denton, Trump described Paxton as “one of the most loyal people,” adding: “Ken Paxton was at my side more than anybody, and I have to always remember that because he could be a pain in the a** sometimes to be honest.” Referring to Talarico, the president said: “To put a guy, a freak like that in there would be such a horror to your state, and such a horror to the country. “We need the votes, and I’m here for that, and I think we’re going to win.” Leaked Audio On Wednesday, the New York Times published leaked audio which it said revealed Paxton telling conservative donors and lobbyists that Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas had damaged his campaign. In the audio, someone asks, “Do you feel like he’s a little bit of a drag?” to which the man purported to be Paxton replies: “So to be honest with you, the numbers, when we did that convention, it dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good.” When approached for comment by The New York Times, Nick Maddux, a senior Paxton advisor, said: “This is more manipulated nonsense from The New York Times to create a story that doesn’t exist.” At the convention, held in Dallas at the American Airlines Center on September 9 and 10, Trump backed Paxton while also mocking his dress sense and appearance. The president said: “He may not dress right. He may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen, but you know what he is? He’s the greatest attorney general in America, and he deserves to be your next senator.” Candidate Controversies & Differences Paxton beat incumbent Republican Senator John Cornyn in a May Texas Republican runoff with the backing of Trump. The contest was bitter, with Cornyn branding his opponent “a known con man and a fraud,” and the senator has since said he won’t campaign for Paxton in November’s election. Impeachment Paxton was impeached by the GOP-controlled Texas House in 2023 over allegations of abuse of public trust and unfitness for office, though he was found not guilty by the state Senate. He consistently denied wrongdoing during this process. Religion However, Talarico has also come under fire over controversial comments related to religion, including his 2021 argument that “God is nonbinary” and is “both Masculine and feminine, and everything in between.” AI According to campaign proposals, Talarico supports an "AI Dividend" that would give Americans a share of the profits from artificial intelligence, while Paxton has called for restrictions on Chinese technology in U.S. data centers and stricter accountability measures for AI products that threaten children's safety. See how each sitting member scores on Newsweek's AI Scorecard. Marijuana Talarico, who supports legalizing and regulating marijuana for adults, has described Texas' restrictions as a "gift to the drug cartels," whereas Paxton has sued multiple cities over cannabis decriminalization measures, saying he will not "stand idly by" while local governments "violate Texas law and promote the use of illicit drugs." Recent Polling Polling conducted over the past few weeks has given Talarico a narrow lead over Paxton, though often within the margin of error. A Rasmussen Reports survey of 1,128 Texas likely voters from 28-29 September put Talarico on 46 percent, one point ahead of Paxton’s 45 percent, with a three percentage point margin of error. Separately, a Texas Public Opinion Research poll gave Talarico a 5-point lead, with 49 percent of the vote to Paxton’s 44 percent. This survey, of 1,007 likely voters over 19-22 September, had a 3.6 point margin of error. As of October 2, the prediction market Polymarket gave Talarico a 62 percent chance of winning the seat, against 39 percent for Paxton. news.title: Shock poll just put one of GOP’s must-win states in play
news.text:
Democrat David Jolly has built a 26-point lead over Republican Byron Donalds among voters in Broward County, according to a new poll offering a fresh look at one of the places Democrats will count on heavily in Florida’s increasingly competitive governor’s race.

According to South Florida’s Sun Sentinel, the Bendixen & Amandi International survey found Jolly ahead of Donalds 52 percent to 26 percent in Broward, one of Florida’s largest and most reliably Democratic counties.

The result is not a statewide poll, and Broward was always expected to favor Jolly. Kamala Harris carried the county by about 17 points in the 2024 presidential election. Still, Jolly’s 26-point advantage gives Democrats the kind of cushion they would want in South Florida if they hope to overcome Republicans’ statewide voter-registration advantage.

It also arrives at a moment when the race for governor no longer looks as comfortable for Republicans as it once did. The Cook Political Report moved the contest from “Likely Republican” to “Lean Republican” this week, citing a tightening race between Jolly and Donalds.

For Jolly, Broward is familiar political territory in another sense. The former Republican congressman left the GOP years ago and eventually joined the Democratic Party, making his political transformation a constant part of the campaign.

Donalds, meanwhile, has campaigned as a conservative successor to Gov. Ron DeSantis and has enjoyed strong financial backing heading into the final stretch.

The Broward poll also found voters narrowly supporting Amendment 3, the property tax proposal that will appear on Florida’s November ballot.

The measure would dramatically increase the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes, beginning with an increase from $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and then to $250,000 in 2028. It needs 60 percent statewide support to pass.

The issue has opened another clear divide between the two candidates.

Donalds supports the amendment and has argued that homeowners deserve relief after years of rising property tax bills.

“The reason why I support Amendment Three is because property taxes have almost doubled in the state the past several years, personal budgets haven’t doubled,” Donalds said this week.

Jolly opposes it, warning that such a steep reduction in local tax revenue could hurt counties that depend on property taxes to pay for services. He has instead pushed for more targeted relief, including help for first-time homebuyers.

For now, the Broward numbers show Jolly doing what a Democrat needs to do in one of Florida’s bluest corners: building a large lead. The harder question is whether he can carry enough of that strength beyond Broward to make the statewide race just as uncomfortable for Donalds.

news.title: GOP in Striking Distance of Flipping 7 States Despite Trump's Low Approval
news.text: Republicans are close to flipping seven Democratic-held Senate and gubernatorial seats in the 2026 midterms, despite President Donald Trump’s falling approval rating creating a challenging national environment for the GOP. Historically, the party of the president loses seats in the midterms when he is unpopular, and Trump’s approval has fallen to record lows in recent polls, fueling Democrats’ optimism about their chances of having a strong night on November 3. But Republicans are still competitive in several Democratic-held seats that could buck the national trend and flip into GOP hands. Four Senate races and three gubernatorial races present flip opportunities for Republicans in this year's midterms. Those include the Senate races in Georgia, Michigan, Minnesota, and New Hampshire, as well as the governor’s races in Kansas, Oregon and Wisconsin. Trump's Approval Rating Creates Headwinds for Republicans in Midterms The national environment is currently favoring Democrats for the midterms, according to recent polling data. A recent survey from YouGov and The Economist found that Democrats have a 15-point advantage on the generic ballot, 53 percent to 38 percent, among likely voters. It surveyed 1,003 likely voters from September 25 to 28. Democrats had an 8.3-point generic ballot lead in RealClearPolitics’ polling average as of Friday. That is approaching Democrats’ generic ballot win of 8.6 points in the 2018 election, the last time there was a "blue wave" election in the popular vote. If that lead holds, Democrats would be well-positioned to take control of the House and compete for Senate control. That is being driven by Trump’s poor approval rating, as well as ongoing frustration with the economy and cost-of-living. In the YouGov poll, Trump’s approval stood at -26 points, 62 percent disapproving and 36 percent approving of his job performance. Meanwhile, only 27 percent of respondents said the country is heading in the right direction, while 23 percent described the economy as being excellent or good. Affordability has become a major theme of the midterms, and that conversation has become dominated by soaring gas prices, which have become a sore spot for Republicans. Gas prices surged amid the Iran war, which has seen disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz, a critical passageway for the global oil supply. Gas prices averaged $4.396 per gallon on Friday, adding pressure to Americans’ wallets as they weigh whether to support Democrats and Republicans. Why Some Democratic-Held Seats Are Still Competitive The national environment can be a powerful force in midterm elections, but there are other factors that can shape an outcome as well. Local issues and dynamics, as well as candidate quality, can keep seats competitive, defying the broader political environment. Many of these seats are in states that are roughly divided between Democrats and Republicans that only narrowly backed either Trump or former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election, meaning there is still a significant GOP voter base in those states. Kansas is more conservative, so any Democratic victory requires candidates to win more conservative voters, even in a strong year for Democrats. Meanwhile, Oregon is more Democratic, and that race could come down to local issues like the economy or educational issues. Senate Seats Republicans Could Flip in Midterms Four Democratic-held Senate races have been competitive in recent polls. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate, so Democrats need to flip four seats to win a majority. But if Republicans manage to flip one of these four seats, Democrats’ already-difficult path to the Senate would become even more narrow, as they would have to win seats in more conservative states to make up for those losses. Newsweek reached out to the campaigns in Michigan, Minnesota and New Hampshire for comment via email. Georgia Georgia is a swing state that narrowly backed Trump in 2024, so Republicans have sought to make its Senate race competitive this year. It's part of the battleground, but Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, has still established a polling lead over Republican Representative Mike Collins. The Cook Political Report has shifted the race to Likely Democratic status. While Georgia was viewed as being more Republican for much of the 2000s, growth in the metro Atlanta area, as well as its suburbs shifting leftward, have turned it more purple. Some of its suburbs were some of the only places in the country that shifted left from 2020 to 2024. Ossoff is viewed as a strong incumbent in Georgia, and given that it only narrowly backed Trump in 2024, Democrats are hopeful a blue-wave environment would keep the seat in their hands. The latest polls favor Ossoff. An InsiderAdvantage poll showed him leading by 8 points, 50 percent to 42 percent. It surveyed 1,200 likely voters from September 22 to 23. The latest YouGov poll gave Ossoff a 10-point advantage, 52 percent to 42 percent. It surveyed 3,301 likely voters from September 15 to 18, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.7 percentage points. Michigan The Michigan Senate race has emerged as one of the most competitive Senate races of the 2026 midterm elections. The state backed Trump by about 1.4 points in 2024 after narrowly backing former President Joe Biden in 2020, so it is one of the most closely divided battlegrounds. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive public health official, is running against Republican former Representative Mike Rogers to succeed retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters. Democrats have hoped the national environment would keep swing states like Michigan in their hands, but polls continue to suggest a close race. Republicans are hoping to flip the race, and have argued El-Sayed is too progressive for a swing state. The latest Fox News poll showed El-Sayed up a single point, 50 percent to 49 percent, while a Marist University survey showed him up 7 points, 51 percent to 44 percent. The Fox News poll, conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research, surveyed 1,028 likely voters from September 24 to 28 with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. The Marist poll surveyed 1,235 registered voters from September 24 to 27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a toss-up. Minnesota Minnesota is more of a Democratic-leaning state, backing Harris by just over 4 points in 2024. It’s another state where Democrats believe the national environment should benefit them, but Republicans still are hoping to make a play for the race to succeed retiring Democratic Senator Tina Smith. Polls have suggested a closer-than-expected race between Democratic Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan and Republican Michele Tafoya, though polling has generally been a bit more limited on the race. Flanagan held a single-point lead in a recent InsiderAdvantage poll, 46 percent to 45 percent, which surveyed 1,200 likely voters from September 28 to 29, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.95 percentage points. Meanwhile, the two candidates were tied in a SurveyUSA poll sponsored by KSTP-TV, each receiving 42 percent of the vote. It surveyed 654 likely voters from September 9 to 14, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. Republicans have sought to tie Flanagan to a fraud scandal that brought scrutiny toward Governor Tim Walz’s administration. The scandal centered around the Feeding Our Future nonprofit, which was implicated in a $250 million COVID-era scheme involving fraudulent claims for child nutrition programs. The Justice Department’s probe, which began under the Biden administration, has led to dozens of indictments. In light of the scandal, Minnesota became the epicenter of the Trump administration’s ramped-up immigration enforcement earlier this year. Two American citizens, Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti, were fatally shot by federal immigration officers in January amid protests in Minneapolis, fueling anger over the White House's hard-line approach to immigration and border security. These are two of the most critical issues facing Minnesota voters in November. Maddie Heinz, a Flanagan spokesperson, told Newsweek that Tafoya is "just another MAGA Republican who will do Trump’s bidding." "Minnesotans showed the world how to stand up to Donald Trump and we’re going to do it again in November," Heinz said. The Cook Political Report classifies it as Likely Democratic. New Hampshire The Senate race in New Hampshire, which backed Harris by fewer than 3 points in 2024, presents another opportunity for Republicans to chip away at a Democratic-held Senate seat. Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen is retiring, and Democratic Representative Chris Pappas and former Senator John Sununu are running to succeed her. Although the state leans toward Democrats, polling of the race is close, and the Cook Political Report recently moved the race into its toss-up category. Sununu, who is part of a well-known and popular political family in the Granite State, is seen as a top recruit for Republicans who can turn a race that should favor Democrats into a true toss-up. Pappas led Sununu by 5 points in a recent poll from The New York Times and Siena University, 50 percent to 45 percent. It surveyed 613 likely voters from September 15 to 22, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.8 percentage points. A poll from the University of New Hampshire gave Pappas an 8-point lead, 50 percent to 42 percent, among likely voters. It was conducted from September 17 to 21 among 1,392 likely voters. Governor Races Republicans Could Flip in Midterms Three gubernatorial races could also flip in November. Generally speaking, governor races are seen as being less defined by traditional partisanship than federal races. This is why solidly Democratic states like Vermont have a Republican governor, while conservative states like Kentucky are more willing to elect a Republican governor. This year, there are three Democratic-held governor seats that appear competitive in the polls. Kansas Kansas, where Governor Laura Kelly cannot run again due to term limits, presents Republicans a clear pickup opportunity. The Sunflower State backed Trump by 16 points in 2024 and is typically seen as a fairly conservative state, though some polling suggests it looks more competitive this year. Republican Ty Masterson is running against Democrat Cindy Holscher to succeed Kelly, and the Cook Political Report classifies the race as Lean Republican, meaning Masterson is seen as having a slight, but not definitive, advantage. An Emerson College poll showed him up 7 points, 51 percent to 44 percent. It surveyed 750 Kansans from September 15 to 16, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. Garrett Henson, Masterson campaign spokesman, told Newsweek that Holscher is "wrong for Kansas," pointing to her position on income taxes, property taxes and transgender athletes. Henson also touted Masterson’s endorsement from labor union SMART-TD, local businessowners, agribusiness and "Kansans of every party in every corner of the state." "It's why Ty is leading in every independent poll," Henson said. "Kansans want a governor who will lower their costs, and that's exactly what Ty will do." Oregon The Oregon gubernatorial race has also become competitive in the polls, despite the fact that Harris carried the state by 14 points in 2024. Governor Tina Kotek is running for reelection and is facing a challenge from Republican Christine Drazan, who lost to Kotek by fewer than 4 points in the 2022 gubernatorial race. A poll from DHM Research gave Drazan a single-point lead, 47 percent to 46 percent. It surveyed 915 likely voters from September 17 to 27, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.24 percentage points, reported Oregon Public Broadcasting. It found that most voters—58 percent—view the state as being on the wrong track, with only 29 percent saying it’s moving in the right direction. A GOP victory in Oregon would be one of the most unexpected midterm results due to its status as a solidly Democratic state, driven by progressive strongholds like Portland. Republicans have not won a gubernatorial race in Oregon since 1982, when the state reelected GOP Governor Victor Atiyeh. A DHM Research survey for the business-backed group Grow Oregon in early September had Drazan ahead 45 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 600 likely voters from September 3 to 9. The Cook Political Report has shifted the race from Likely Democrat to Lean Democrat, a sign that they view it as becoming more competitive for Republicans. Wisconsin Republicans also see an opportunity in Wisconsin, a swing state that backed Trump by 0.9 points in 2024, the closest state for either party in the 2024 election. Democratic Governor Tony Evers is not running for another term. Republican Representative Tom Tiffany won his party’s nomination, while Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley emerged victorious from the Democratic primary after exiting, and later reentering the race, amid concerns about the then-frontrunner state legislator Francesca Hong, a Democratic Socialist. Wisconsin is generally a closely divided state that is competitive in most cycles, and Republicans are investing in the race. According to a report from Wisconsin Public Radio, Tiffany raised $26 million in the last quarter, the majority of the haul coming from three billionaire Republican megadonors. The latest Marquette University Law School poll showed a tight race between the two candidates, with Crowley leading by 3 points, 49 percent to 46 percent. It surveyed 692 likely voters from September 16 to 23, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.8 percentage points. The race is classified as a toss-up by the Cook Political Report. Recent Midterms Show States Can Defy National Trends There have been outliers in recent midterms, where some states have defied the national headwinds to flip against the party benefiting from the national environment. The 2022 midterms were generally a good year for Republicans, but Democrats still managed to flip several seats. Democrat John Fetterman flipped a Senate seat in Pennsylvania, a key battleground, while Democrats also flipped three governorships. That includes Massachusetts and Maryland, two Democratic-leaning states where voters previously split their tickets for moderate Republican governors, and the swing state Arizona. In 2018, Republicans flipped four Senate seats in Florida, Indiana, Missouri and North Dakota despite an environment favoring Democrats. Although Florida was close in 2016, the other three states voted for Trump by wide margins despite having Democratic incumbents and were seen as uphill battles at the time. Cook’s latest outlook has the race for control in the Senate as a true toss-up, with Democrats projected to gain one to five seats; they need a net gain of 4 to take the majority. news.summary: Seven states could defy headwinds to elect Republicans to seats currently held by Democrats in the midterms, according to polls.

Alas, on Thursday, whiffs of Gibson in U.S. policy started haunting headlines again—that is, when PunchUp, a Substack affiliated with the Daily Beast, revealed some disturbing new intel, via a former Justice Department lawyer that got fired in May. 

To be clear, we’ve known since last month that while the DOJ was rolling out its Federal Firearm Rights Restoration Program—a Trump-era policy that sought to restore gun ownership for felons or convicted criminals who could qualify—former Pardon Attorney Elizabeth Oyer was allegedly fired in 2025 for refusing to let Gibson qualify, in particular. But per PunchUp, Oyer also said a senior official at the department told her she explicitly couldn’t not bend the rules for Gibson because it was “necessary to grant relief” to him as “Mr. Gibson had a personal relationship with President Trump.” Gross. 

Ahead of her firing, Oyer also said last year that she was directed by Blanche—then a deputy AG—to include Gibson on a list with nine others that should have had their gun rights restored. Her pushback, she later said, was because letting him own a gun was “not something that [she] could recommend lightly.” AG Pam Bondi restored his rights that same year.

As we know, Gibson has long been a loud and proud stan of Trump, and during the 2024 election, compared Kamala Harris’ intelligence to a “fence post.” Days after he entered office, Trump rewarded Gibson for the cronyism by appointing him—alongside Jon Voight and Sylvester Stallone—ambassadors to Hollywood. 

Oyer was fired in 2025, though the DOJ in March did deny the connection between her pushback on Gibson and her firing. In May, government watchdog CREW (Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington) reported that more than 600 officials have been fired or forced out under Trump’s leadership, estimating also about 6,000 years of expertise lost as a result. A compilation of their farewell messages, collected by the Justice Connection, shows many of them also stepped down for refusing to bend to the administration’s animus-driven agendas. “I will not…serve this current incarnation of the Department,” one attorney wrote. “It defines ‘justice’ in a way that I do not recognize.”

This is the second (known) time Gibson’s appeared to stink up real policy.

news.title: The Patriot Post® · A Leaner Federal Workforce Is a Win for Taxpayers
news.text:
One of the most unheralded policy successes of President Donald Trump’s second term has been the purging of many unnecessary federal jobs.

The federal government has reduced its workforce by 300,000 jobs since Jan. 20, 2025, bringing it down to a still-bulky 2.7 million employees. Not since President Lyndon Johnson’s Great Society vastly expanded the scope of the national government has the federal workforce been at this level.

It’s not merely that the feds have shed superfluous jobs — there are still over 4 million contract workers, after all. It’s that the White House has been targeting all the right institutions.

The bloated War Department, with over 61,000 departures, and the equally bloated State Department, with 37% of its staff gone, experienced the biggest reductions.

But most of the buyouts were aimed at agencies and departments that should have been shuttered a long time ago. Take the U.S. Agency for International Development, which, for years, was used to funnel billions to hard-left ideological projects around the world. Virtually its entire staff is gone.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the unaccountable bureaucratic brainchild of progressive Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), has lost roughly 88% of its workers, though it’s still far too big.

The Agriculture Department, which, despite its name, is principally a welfare agency that has little to do with farming, experienced tens of thousands of departures. So has another welfare-state institution, the Department of Housing and Urban Development, whose most notable achievement has been helping inflate housing prices.

Not every agency is being clipped fast enough, though. Early in his term, Trump signed an executive order directing the dismantling of the Education Department. Yet this intrusive agency, which spends its time propping up unions and undermining local initiatives, has lost only 40% of its staff.

Every time Republicans threaten to cut federal jobs, though they rarely follow through, Democrats predict that society will be plunged into chaos and high unemployment.

The unemployment rate in September 2024 was 4.1%. In September 2025, it was 4.4%. It’s at 4.1% today. Barely anyone, one suspects, has noticed that the federal workforce has shrunk by around 11%. They probably wouldn’t notice if it shrank by another 11%.

What Democrats really fear is losing power. Federal agencies, government employees and public-sector unions are all bases of political influence for the Left.

“This is an attempt at intimidation,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) complained when the Office of Management and Budget released a memo instructing agencies to plan for large-scale layoffs. “Donald Trump has been firing federal workers since day one — not to govern, but to scare.”

Why would Democrats be “scared” of a leaner federal workforce?

We don’t know how government employees vote, but we can make an educated guess. Around 84% of campaign donations from federal workers went to Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris in 2024. Federal civilian jobs rose by over 130,000 under the Biden administration. Around 11% of the approximately 16 million jobs added during Biden’s term were federal, state and local government jobs. Roughly 15% of the total workforce, around 24 million people, still work for the government at all levels.

There is more that can be done, not only in trimming the federal workforce but also in decentralizing and dispersing it. The Trump administration promised to relocate more federal jobs out of the Washington area. The political class entrenched around the capital in Virginia and Maryland keeps voting to empower itself. It should be dispersed as much as possible. 

In 2001, anti-tax activist Grover Norquist famously proclaimed that his goal was to shrink the federal government until it was small enough to “drag it into the bathroom and drown it in the bathtub.” We’ve learned over the years that it doesn’t work that way. Neither party has any plan to curb spending, and voters don’t seem to be clamoring for one.

Shrinking the federal bureaucracy and workforce isn’t going to restrain massive deficit spending and our economy-threatening, turbocharged debt. Still, paring down the size, scope and intrusiveness of a swollen federal government, even if it’s just temporary until Democrats come back into power, is a win for taxpayers.

news.title: NY GOP Rep. Mike Lawler leads Dem Cait Conley in key battleground House district: new internal poll
news.text:
Hudson Valley Rep. Mike Lawler (R-NY) has pulled ahead of his Democratic rival Cait Conley by a narrow three points in the neck-and-neck battleground race, new internal polling shared exclusively with The Post shows.

The incumbent GOP pol leads with 50% of the vote compared with Conley’s 47% in the 17th Congressional District battle, according to the Lawler campaign’s internal poll of 400 likely voters, conducted Sept. 28 to 30.

The poll, administered by McLaughlin & Associates, has a margin of error of 4.9% — further evidence of the key race remaining a true toss-up.

The new survey comes a day after a PIX 11 and Emerson College poll showed Conley — a West Point grad and Biden administration national security official — with a razor-thin two-point lead over Lawler.

The Emerson-PIX 11 poll was conducted Sept. 27 to 29.

The Lawler campaign poll showed the second-term congressman up 92% to Conley’s 6% among Republicans, and up 52% to Conley’s 40% amongst independents.

It also shows Lawler with a considerable 20% of Democrats, to Conley’s 79%.

The 17th District, covering Westchester, Rockland, Putnam and Dutchess Counties, was carried by former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 and is one of Democrats’ most sought-after pickups in November’s midterm elections.

Lawler’s survey also included polling showing GOP gubernatorial nominee Bruce Blakeman leading Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul 51% to 47% in the key suburban district.

Blakeman did slightly better than Lawler among independents with 55% to Hochul’s 37%.
news.summary: The incumbent GOP pol leads with 50% of the vote compared with Conley's 47% in the 17th Congressional District battle, according to the Lawler campaign's internal poll of 400 likely voters.

news.title: Michigan fraudster — once honored by Biden — posed as US ambassador, bank owner to steal $1M from victims to fund lavish lifestyle
news.text:
Call her Money Steal.

A Detroit businesswoman, once honored by President Joe Biden, allegedly posed as a US ambassador and a banker to con several victims out of over $1 million to fund her lavish lifestyle.

Shannon Monet Steel claimed to be the Ambassador to the First Lady of the Central African Republic, a hotel owner and a banker with $350 million in assets to fool her victims in her years-long scheme, federal prosecutors accused, according to the Detroit News on Wednesday.

Steel, 42, was arrested and slapped with fraud charges after allegedly targeting at least eight victims between 2022 and 2026, according to court documents obtained by the outlet.

The Detroit “mogul” curated her online life as a high-rolling, prominent leader, showing off multiple awards and recognitions, her interactions with high-profile politicians and international trips.

Steel is accused of swindling her first victim, a California investor, when she forged a false “Bank confirmation letter” from Deutsche Bank and claimed her own bank, Steel Private Bank, held over 300,000,000 euros.

The falsified letter convinced the victim to wire $200,000 to an escrow account in exchange for a Standby Letter of Credit, the charging documents alleged.

Bank officials later determined the “bank confirmation letter” was a fake.

Officials also discovered Steel Private Bank was registered in the US and wasn’t FDIC insured.

Steel used her self-named “entities” to defraud at least $1.05 million from eight others by assuring them millions in loans from Steel Private Bank but instead “pocketing the good faith escrow funds” from the trusting victims, officials claimed in an Emergency Ex-Parte motion filed with the US District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan on Sept. 10.

Steel used the funds to rent and lease several luxury cars, including a 2022 Maserati Levante and a 2013 Bentley Coupe that cost upwards of $215,000, the outlet reported.

She also paid off credit cards and used $56,000 to rent a home in Northville Township, Mich.

Steel documented her life on social media, promoting herself as Ambassador Steel, wearing merchandise of her fake bank and sharing accomplishments for her false work that earned her national recognition.

“As the newly appointed Ambassador for the First Lady of C.A.R. NGO on a mission to eradicate poverty, I am committed to developing economic stability in the Central African Republic by providing the necessary essentials to its citizens,” Steel wrote on her Shannon Steel Foundation website. 

“My top priority is to represent the country’s history, ideals, and interests. To do so, I am aware of the expectations and will strive to meet them to the best of my ability.

Officials were tipped off to Steel’s fake ambassadorship after a reporter contacted the Department of State trying to verify Steel’s credentials.

In 2024, President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris presented Steel with the Lifetime Presidential Achievement Award. 

Steel shared a poster of the award that labeled her as the CEO of Steel Private Bank, Ambassador and Hedge Fund Owner.

The achievement was “certified by President Biden” as part of the President’s Volunteer Service Awards program and featured photos of Steel, Biden and Harris.

Steel was presented the award without any documentation that she had completed the required 4,000 hours of lifetime volunteer service, the presenter told investigators.

AmeriCorps, the operator of the awards, told investigators Steel being awarded the achievement was inconsistent with program guidelines and she shouldn’t have been given the award based on the information known at the time.

The fraudster boosted her resume when she claimed she acquired and later renovated an Embassy Suites by Hilton hotel for $3,000,000, flipping it to a Wyndham in Southfield, Mich.

Officials discovered the hotel was never granted a certificate of occupancy and never given the authorization to open.

Ramada Worldwide, Inc. won a default judgment against Steel and other defendants for breach of franchise agreement and was awarded $1,558,444.79, according to the court records.

Steel was framed as a con artist with a history of bankruptcies who has used stolen funds to pay off victims who became suspicious of her antics.

“These allegations are only a relevant summary of what Steel is known to be doing to hide and spend criminal proceeds,” Assistant US Attorney K. Craig Welkener wrote. “Her actual efforts are almost certainly more substantial.”
news.summary: A Detroit businesswoman, once honored by President Joe Biden, allegedly posed as a US ambassador and a banker to con several victims out of over $1 million to fund her lavish lifestyle.
