news.title: Toward the Final Stretch — and Beyond
news.text:
Haven't we seen this movie before? Voters, weary of a Republican president whose foreign or domestic policies don't seem to be delivering as promised, seem on the verge of a massive rejection of his party.

Polls show Democrats surging. The generic ballot — which party's candidates would you favor for the House of Representatives? — shows Democrats far ahead of Republicans. Statewide polls show Democrats ahead in large states that had voted Republican for president and threatening incumbents in historically Republican states such as Kansas and Nebraska.

That's pretty much the picture today. Donald Trump's job approval has slipped below 40 percent, below his numbers at the end of September 2018 and similar to George W. Bush's in September 2006.

Republicans trail in the generic vote by about as much as in 2018 and by wider margins in 2006.

All of which provides a strong basis for the professional prognosticators' predictions that Democrats will overturn the Republicans' current narrow majority in the House and some justification for those who say they have a majority chance of gaining the four seats that would give them a majority in the Senate.

But there are a couple of caveats here. Republican pollster Patrick Ruffini points out that polls in the last four congressional elections have understated Republicans' actual election performance by wide margins in the summer, then narrowed in the fall. But this year, there is little sign of such narrowing yet.

But perhaps the polls are consistently understating Republican support, as analyst Nate Silver says they have in the last three presidential elections. Many pollsters report it's much harder to reach Republican respondents, who tend to mistrust media pollsters.

And this year, many Republicans seem unhappy with the president and his party. Does that mean they're just unwilling to be polled or that they will skip voting as well? No one knows the answer.

And no one knows the answer to the question posed by Robert Redford's character in the movie "The Candidate" when he wins the election: "What do we do now?" No one seems to know for sure what Democrats will do if they win majorities in both houses. A Democrat Senate is unlikely to confirm any Trump appointee to the Supreme Court and probably to any federal court, and would likely extract concessions from any nominee to a high policy position — unless Pennsylvania's John Fetterman denies Democrats their 51st vote.

Democratic majorities might try to cabin Trump's power to set tariffs, but they won't be able to change underlying trade statutes and must depend on the courts to decide, as they have already in some cases, that those laws don't justify Trump's actions.

Democrats may also try to end U.S. military operations against Iran, which, in any case, have been erratic. But they may not be able to. Bush was able to execute his successful surge strategy in Iraq, despite majority opposition in both houses after Democrats' victories in the off-year elections in 2006.

One gets little sense from the campaign dialogue what Democratic majorities would aim to do on other policies. Their candidates decry high gas prices and inflation generally. But they're unlikely to revert to the Biden administration's policy, prompted by the COVID-19 pandemic, of vastly expanding federal spending, which resulted in 9 percent inflation in 2022 and remained a continuing liability for Joe Biden and Kamala Harris in 2024.

There's a general impulse in the Democrat Party to see the working class as its core constituency and to respond to its presumed needs with economic redistribution. That's the lesson Democrats take from Franklin Roosevelt and the rich literature inspired by his New Deal.

But the impulse is outdated. The white college graduate voters who now dominate Democrat primaries and fundraising may indulge the marxist and progressive presumption that the working class is especially morally worthy, but they can hardly help observing that blue-collar workers have been voting increasingly Republican even before Trump rode down his escalator.

Indeed, as economist and former Sen. Phil Gramm has shown, the United States already has economic redistribution policies locked into place, so that the bottom 60 percent of income earners are eligible for government transfer payments, raising them to average income levels.

In those circumstances, Biden's major push toward redistribution was his frequent proposals (sometimes overruled, like Trump's tariffs, by the courts) for forgiveness of college and graduate student loans. The beneficiaries of those loans were not only the gender studies majors looking for adjunct work but also the gaggles of college and university administrators subsidized by those programs.

It's interesting that the Biden administration, staffed not only at the top but throughout with Obama administration veterans, did not seek a highly visible overhaul of healthcare financing.

They surely remember the political price they paid for Obamacare. Passed only by parliamentary legerdemain in the face of adverse polling, it saw Republicans gain 64 House seats in the 2010 off-year election. That was the biggest off-year gain for either party since Bill Clinton broke Republicans' lock on the presidency in 1992 and Newt Gingrich broke Democrats' lock on the House in 1994.

Defenders of Obamacare may respond that Republicans' attempts to repeal it were unpopular and were defeated by John McCain's vote in 2018. But tying together the broad opposition to Obamacare during Barack Obama's tenure with the broad opposition to Obamacare repeal during Trump's is the fact that large majorities of the public, for all their grumblings, are content with their current healthcare financing and oppose any attempts to take it away.

That's something Democrats may want to consider when they see young Democratic Socialists of America support Bernie Sanders' Medicare for All proposal. By definition, it would eliminate the arrangements most Americans have made and are content with. Lots of voters are not going to like that.

American voters generally, and Democrat politicians in particular, tend to look to government to cure various ills. In that perspective, you can argue — and certainly public opinion polls would suggest most people would — that the nation's performance in this first quarter of the 21st century has been suboptimal.

But the mostly unanticipated performance of the private sector has been better, in technological devices and communication and in fracking technology, which has made the U.S. once again the world's greatest oil producer, as it was at the outset of World War II. Elon Musk has outperformed the heavily regulated Detroit Three in making a profitable business of building electric cars and has outperformed government-run NASA at producing reusable space rockets.

Looking back over the century so far, the historian Niall Ferguson admits, "My prophetic vision of decline and fall 25 years ago clearly has not been fulfilled. In relative terms, America is still Number One by any measure except maybe the number of robots." That despite the disappointments and demerits of successive administrations and Congresses. Whether the Democrats sweep the off-year elections next month or the Republicans once again outpoll the polls, the winners — and losers — might want to keep that perspective in mind.

news.title: Sleeper Senate race emerges as unexpected headache for Republicans ahead of midterms
news.text: Republicans fully acknowledge that they are facing political headwinds going into the midterm elections in November, and those winds are swirling in a race that has become quietly competitive as Election Day nears. Kansas has, for nearly a century, consistently elected Republicans to the Senate. But in a midterm election year when voters are unhappy with the Trump administration’s actions and its impacts on the economy, the race between Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton has tightened more than some in the GOP would have liked. Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., the Senate GOP’s campaign chief, acknowledged that the race is close, but remained confident Marshall would hold on. Republicans are trying to maintain and grow their 53-seat majority, but face many toss-up contests across the map, and voters that are frustrated with high fuel prices, tariffs and the war in Iran, that could threaten that grip on power. Kansas isn’t in that toss-up category, but it was recently downgraded by "Likely Republican" to "Lean Republican" by the Cook Political Report and in Fox News’ election power rankings. Notably, Kansas is the third-largest cattle producer in the country. "Some of the things that we grow, because we like to eat them, like cattle, end up producing more carbon dioxide than other crops that we could grow, other forms of food that we could have," Hamilton said. news.title: Democratic surge predicted to hit Republican states hardest, scrambling Senate strategy
news.text:
WASHINGTON: Kentucky Democrats say they have a once-in-a-generation opportunity to flip a US Senate seat in a Republican stronghold. But a couple of things are missing: their governor and money.

Kentucky is one of several states that President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024 ​where Republicans are significantly trailing the president’s performance, an indication that Democrats have expanded their pathway to a majority in November’s midterm elections. It’s not clear, however, that the party will invest its limited resources into flipping seats once considered to be out of reach.

The Democratic surge looks strongest in states Trump won by wide margins, though Republicans are also significantly underperforming in Georgia and North Carolina, where Trump won by 2 and 3 percentage points, respectively. The volume of unexpectedly competitive states could scramble the final stretch of the campaign cycle as top officials assess where to spend their war chests.

“Not only is there a swing away from the Republican Party compared to 2024, but the swing actually seems to be somewhat bigger in red America than in blue America, and that’s putting these states that Trump won easily very much into play,” said David Hopkins, a political science professor at Boston College.

Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority and entered the political cycle with a favorable map to maintain control of the chamber for the final two years of Trump’s presidency. But less than five weeks out from Election Day, polling shows Democrats are competitive in 10 states Trump won by double digits in 2024: Ohio, Alaska, Iowa, Texas, Florida, Kansas, Nebraska, Mississippi, South Carolina and ‌Kentucky.

To win the Senate, ‌Democrats must defend two seats in states Trump carried and win four Republican-held seats, including at least two in states Trump won by ​double ‌digits. Ohio, ⁠Alaska, Iowa and ​Texas ⁠have largely been viewed as Senate battlegrounds this cycle, but the political environment is so poor for Republicans that Democrat Adam Hamilton is narrowly leading US Senator Roger Marshall in recent polls in Kansas, which Trump won by 16 percentage points.

Democratic candidates Angie Nixon of Florida and Annie Andrews of South Carolina are running neck and neck against Republican incumbents in recent polls, which show Democratic-aligned candidates in Nebraska, Mississippi and Kentucky trailing by single digits. Trump carried those states by margins ranging from 13 in Florida to 31 in Kentucky. He told reporters on Monday that “the polls are fake.”

Polls capture voter sentiments but don’t necessarily predict election outcomes. Several primary polls, for example, showed Francesca Hong leading by 20 or more points in the Democratic primary for Wisconsin governor. She lost by less than 1 percent.

Republicans say they aren’t taking anything for granted this cycle. US Senator Tim Scott, who chairs Senate Republicans’ campaign arm, said Republicans are running in “a record number of toss-up races,” and money won’t be a problem. The party’s top candidates are being supported by hundreds of millions of dollars in outside spending.

“Cash is king,” Scott told reporters ⁠on Wednesday. “It’s a powerful tool that is providing us with the firepower necessary to really share our message, and our message is incredibly important for ‌us to win these races.”

Kentucky race tightens

Democrat Charles Booker’s internal polling has him within single digits of US Representative Andy Barr in ‌the race to succeed longtime Republican US Senator Mitch McConnell of Kentucky. But Barr has a $2 million cash advantage over Booker, whose allies ​say Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, could give him the boost he ‌needs to win.

“We have a shot here in Kentucky to flip this seat, and we need to do it now,” said Pamela Stevenson, minority floor leader of the Kentucky House.

Eric Hyers, Beshear’s 2019 and ‌2023 campaign manager who helps run his In This Together PAC, said the governor has already endorsed Booker.

“They’ll likely be together at get-out-the-vote events down the homestretch of the campaign,” Hyers said.

Political prognosticators have shifted some races toward Democrats in deeply Republican states, but many of these expansion seats maintain ratings that view them as solidly Republican or likely to remain Republican. The White House is deploying Trump to these states in an apparent effort to juice base turnout in November.

The president will visit Texas and campaign in Oklahoma on Thursday, followed by rallies in Alabama on Friday, Ohio on Saturday and Nebraska on Monday. Trump won Oklahoma by 34 points, Texas by 14, Alabama by 31, Ohio by ‌11 and Nebraska by 21. His approval rating has fallen to a historic low of 32 percent, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll, while his war with Iran and tariffs have driven up prices as voters have consistently highlighted the cost of living as their top concern ahead of the midterms. ⁠That likely makes him more of a liability than ⁠an asset in traditional battlegrounds, political analysts say.

Democrats see expanded senate map

Democrats say they have transformed the map of races in play.

“Our goal has always been a Democratic Senate majority, and the pathways to get there have only gotten bigger since the start of the cycle,” said Lauren French, a spokesperson for Senate Majority PAC, a Democratic super PAC. Super PACs can raise and spend unlimited sums but cannot coordinate with candidates, campaigns or party committees.

French said Republicans have diverted resources from Georgia and North Carolina to Republican strongholds, where she said Republicans are starting to talk about gas prices and other costs.

While some Republicans have leaned into culture war issues such as transgender athletes in girls’ and women’s sports, other Republicans have begun distancing themselves from the Trump administration. That includes Republicans in states such as Kansas and Mississippi, where US Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith acknowledged in a social media video last week that fuel cost was her constituents’ top issue.

“I feel it, too, every time I fill up my truck to get around the state,” she said. “This administration is working to end the conflict of Iran, which will ultimately lower the price of fuel.”

Money remains uncertain factor

Republicans are already outspending Democrats by millions of dollars — tens of millions in some cases — on future ad reservations in Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Alaska and Kansas, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.

Republicans in reach states — Republican strongholds that could flip to Democrats in a wave election — also have significant financial advantages over their opponents, with the exception of South Carolina, where Andrews entered July with more than $4 million on hand. US Senator Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat in July after the death of her brother US Senator Lindsey Graham, won ​the Republican nomination in an August special primary runoff but reported having just $250,000 as of August ​5.

Rufus Gifford, former finance chair for Joe Biden’s and Kamala Harris’ presidential campaigns, said there are strategic advantages to Democrats investing in expansion states, such as forcing Republicans to play defense in areas they didn’t expect.

“The truth is that many of these states have been fool’s gold for Democrats for a very, very long time,” he said. But “there’s very little doubt that we have a shot in some of these even more reach states.”

news.title: Republicans are losing support among Latinos. It might cost them the House.
news.text:
In 2024, Donald Trump’s success in appealing to Hispanic working-class voters, particularly young men, fueled his return to the White House and put the political world on notice. Strategists even raised the prospect of a realignment that could give the GOP a formidable edge for years to come.

Just one election cycle later, however, those gains appear to have vanished, and then some.

With fewer than five weeks to go before the Nov. 3 midterms, polls indicate that the Latino voters who had embraced the Republican Party are abandoning it in droves, and at a greater rate than non-Hispanic voters. Increasingly, these voters are telling pollsters that they disapprove of President Trump and that he has failed to deliver on his promise to bring down the cost of living. The prices of gas and groceries are of particular concern, driven up in part by the war with Iran. Many also have soured on the administration’s immigration policies.

The GOP’s collapse among the Hispanic electorate might be particularly costly because many of the most competitive House districts this year – in states from Texas to Florida, and California to Pennsylvania – have high shares of Latino voters, sometimes even majorities. The collapse is also a key reason some previously noncompetitive seats now appear to be in play for Democrats. Heavily Hispanic districts in South Texas, for example, which were gerrymandered to create more seats for the GOP, might now be at risk: A poll of Texas Latino voters found that only one-third approved of Mr. Trump, who won Latinos in Texas by 10 points in 2024.

“Hispanics rented but did not buy Republican in 2024,” says Albert Eisenberg, a GOP political consultant in Pennsylvania who runs outreach programs to Latinos. “Our mistake [since 2024] has been not showing up and delivering for our future Republican voters.”

While some Latinos support Mr. Trump’s border policy, a majority in most polls disapprove of the administration’s immigration enforcement tactics. Last month, Florida Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican from a majority-Hispanic district in Miami, broke publicly with Mr. Trump on immigration, saying in a campaign video that Latinos who voted for Mr. Trump felt “betrayed.”

Latino voters, who make up around 16% of the electorate, are not a monolith. But the hard turn away from Republicans is happening across the country, says Mike Madrid, a Republican political strategist and pollster based in California. “I’m seeing Puerto Ricans in Allentown, Cubans in Miami, Mexicans in the Rio Grande and the Central Valley of California, Dominicans in New Jersey, Central Americans in Virginia, the Manassas area, all moving in the same direction,” he says.

But just as the rightward shift in 2024 didn’t last, he warns, the current move toward Democrats could prove to be transitory as well – with Latinos becoming a true swing constituency. “It’s not really right or left. It’s moving away from both parties,” he says. “It’s a dealignment.”

Pocketbook issues

In Pennsylvania’s 7th Congressional District, which includes Allentown, 1 in 5 residents identify as Hispanic. In 2024, Latino voters here helped Republican Ryan Mackenzie eke out a victory by about 4,000 votes. This year, Democrats have nominated Bob Brooks, a firefighter and union leader, in a race that’s now one of the party’s top pickup opportunities.

Allentown lies in Pennsylvania’s Lehigh Valley, where steel and manufacturing industries first drew workers from Puerto Rico during the expansion that followed World War II. In recent decades, Dominicans, Puerto Ricans, and other Latinos moved here to work in warehouses and other service industries that have replaced most of the manufacturing jobs. Latinos now make up a majority of the nearly 130,000 people in Pennsylvania’s third-largest city.

Some commute to jobs in Philadelphia and New York, trying to make higher wages to afford housing and other essentials. But it’s become harder to make ends meet as costs for gas and other items keep climbing, says Alex Dejesus, the pastor of a bilingual evangelical church in Allentown. He’s seeing more families come to a financial breaking point and reach out for help.

Many are asking, he says, “‘Hey, which bill am I gonna pay this month?’ Or, ‘Which bill am I not gonna pay this month?’”

At Ana Pena’s Dominican restaurant, steaming-hot dishes are served from metal trays behind a plexiglass-fronted counter topped with pumpkin and sunflower paper cutouts. Ms. Pena voted twice for Mr. Trump, but is unhappy with how the president has handled the economy.

“Business is bad because people don’t have money to spend on food,” she says. “We expected prices would come down. But the price of everything is going up.” She says she won’t be voting for Republicans in the midterms.

In 2024, voters blamed inflation and high prices on Democrats, says Allentown Mayor Matt Tuerk, a Democrat who knocked on doors that year for Vice President Kamala Harris. “People didn’t feel like their concerns were being heard by Democrats at the time,” he says.

The result that year was a swing to Republicans in 52 out of 55 city precincts. In Lehigh County, where she held a rally the day before Election Day, Ms. Harris won by fewer than 5,000 votes – a nearly threefold decline from Joe Biden’s margin of victory in 2020.

Still, when Mayor Tuerk checked subsequent voter rolls in Allentown, he saw only a modest uptick in Republican registrations. “It wasn’t a structural shift that I could see,” he says.

A September poll by Franklin & Marshall College in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, found Mr. Brooks with a five-point lead over Mr. Mackenzie, the Republican incumbent, with 16% undecided. A majority of respondents said they were worse off than a year ago.

Disillusionment

Republicans in Allentown say they understand the financial pressures and why voters are disgruntled. But “you have to vote for the right people,” says George Rivera, who chairs the Lehigh County Republican Committee. A vote for Democrats, he says, will mean higher taxes, and that would hurt Latinos who run small businesses in the community.

Mr. Rivera and other Republicans are keen to stress the local issues that Mr. Mackenzie has worked on, rather than talk about Mr. Trump and his agenda. In June, Mr. Mackenzie appeared with the president at a rally at Mack Trucks outside Allentown. But on his campaign website today, there are no images from the rally and no mentions at all of Mr. Trump.

Arnaud Armstrong, a campaign spokesman, says “the choice on affordability is clear.” Mr. Mackenzie “has cut taxes for every American, delivered results for working families, stood up to special interests and big corporations, and brought over $160 million home to the Lehigh Valley and the Poconos.”

For some Latino voters, that remains a compelling message. Luis Garcia, a member of the National Guard, voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 and says he has no regrets. He supports the war against Iran, saying “it had to be addressed,” despite the economic impacts here at home. “I drive a truck. I know what gas costs,” he adds.

He met Mr. Mackenzie at a recent lunch in Allentown for service members and came away impressed, though he says he is still weighing his vote in November.

Mr. Brooks, the Democratic nominee, has strong support from labor unions and migrant advocates. In his pitch to Latinos, he styles himself “Bombero Bob,” using the Spanish word for firefighter. He calls Mr. Mackenzie a “lapdog” for Mr. Trump.

Mr. Mackenzie has supported Trump policies that “cause harm to our community,” says Cristian Pungo, a Democratic city council member in Allentown. But opposing Mr. Trump “only gets you so far” with Latino voters, many of whom are disillusioned both with Democrats and Republicans, he warns. “What are you actually going to do? What is the plan?”

In a statement, Mr. Brooks zeros in on the Iran war. “Latino voters want what everybody wants: a life they can afford and a fair shot at the American dream. Right now, gas prices are making that impossible, and Ryan Mackenzie has voted six times to continue the war in Iran that’s driving them up. I’ll vote to bring it to an end.”

Arturo Rand hasn’t forgotten the George W. Bush administration’s war in Iraq, during which his son served in the Air Force. Until then, the Colombian-born engineer had voted for Republicans. But the Iraq War, waged on the premise of nonexistent weapons of mass destruction, soured him on the GOP.

Mr. Trump “promised many things and has delivered so little,” Mr. Rand says from his neatly swept café in Allentown, where customers can get authentic “Pan de Bono,” a Colombian cheese bread. And he’s outraged at the Trump administration’s treatment of immigrants. “Trump hates us,” he says.

So, when the Brooks campaign offered him yard signs, he agreed to put them outside his café.

He’s faced some criticism over the signs, and briefly wondered whether he should keep his political views private. But he decided against it. “I have to stand for something in my life,” he says.
news.summary: Many of the most competitive House districts this year, in states from Texas to Florida, California to Pennsylvania, have majority or near-majority Latino electorates.

news.title: LA Times Owner's Daughter Slams Paper Over Israeli Tourism Ad's Borderless Map
news.text:
A sponsored Israeli tourism advertisement running on the Los Angeles Times website has drawn public criticism from an unexpected corner: the daughter of the paper's own billionaire owner. Nika Soon-Shiong, 33, says the ad's map of Israel erases the occupied Palestinian territories, and she is not shy about saying so, even though her father, Patrick Soon-Shiong, controls the company that published it.

According to the New York Post, the advertisement appears to depict the West Bank and the occupied Syrian Golan Heights as part of Israel, with no border distinctions shown and landmarks including Jerusalem, Haifa, Acre and Tel Aviv highlighted across the map. Nika Soon-Shiong, who founded Drop Site News in 2024, responded to the ad with a blunt “What on earth?” Her outlet, which she was named publisher of in September 2025, described the map as showing a single borderless Israel stretching from the Mediterranean Sea to the Jordan River.

Nika Soon-Shiong argued the promotion does not break U.S. law but runs contrary to international law, per Drop Site News. The dispute centers on L.A. Times Studios, the commercial arm that produced and ran the ad — a separate company that uses Los Angeles Times branding for advertisements, sponsored content and other non-journalism material, and which is part of the Los Angeles Times Media Group that Patrick Soon-Shiong chairs as chief executive. The campaign, titled “Israel: Land of Creation” and tagged as a Paid Program on latimes.com, promoted a nine-day itinerary across Israel and the occupied territories and was paid for by Israel's Ministry of Tourism.

Newsroom Says It Had No Hand in the Ad

Los Angeles Times reporter James Queally said the newspaper itself was not responsible for the advertisement, but acknowledged that the lack of separation between the Times and L.A. Times Studios frustrates the entire staff. That friction is not abstract: the advertisement's masthead redirects to the Los Angeles Times homepage, and its URL uses the same domain name as the newspaper itself, blurring the line between journalism and paid promotion for readers clicking through.

The episode lands at a moment when the Los Angeles Times editorial operation has already been stretched thin. By March 2025, consecutive rounds of buyouts and layoffs had left the editorial board with no remaining full-time staff writers, with the Los Angeles Times Guild reporting 48 staff departures in that buyout round alone. Patrick Soon-Shiong acquired the Los Angeles Times and the San Diego Union-Tribune from Tronc for $500 million in February 2018, and in July 2025 he announced plans to take the paper public within a year, an effort he said was meant to let readers hold a stake on its board.

A Father-Daughter Rift With a 2024 Precedent

This is not the first time Nika Soon-Shiong has broken publicly with her father's newspaper over Middle East coverage. She has claimed the Los Angeles Times declined to endorse Kamala Harris ahead of the 2024 presidential election, a decision that followed the paper's practice of backing Democratic presidential candidates in every cycle since 2008. Editorials editor Mariel Garza and board members Robert Greene and Karin Klein resigned that October after Patrick Soon-Shiong blocked the planned endorsement.

At the time, Nika Soon-Shiong publicly attributed the blocked endorsement to opposition to the Biden-Harris administration's Gaza policy. Patrick Soon-Shiong responded with a statement saying his daughter speaks in her own personal capacity, has no role at the Los Angeles Times, and does not participate in editorial-board decisions or discussions.

Her advocacy on Middle East press issues extends beyond her father's paper. In June, Nika Soon-Shiong publicly criticized a Committee to Protect Journalists board proposal to redefine “journalist,” calling it a betrayal. Before her media career, she served as a Public Safety Commissioner for the City of West Hollywood from 2021 to 2022 and directed the Fund for Guaranteed Income, which ran basic-income pilots in Compton and Long Beach, before stepping down to finish her doctorate at the University of Oxford.

Questions Remain Over Commercial Policies

Whether the Los Angeles Times will revisit its commercial advertising policies around disputed territorial maps remains an open question, as does how the newsroom Guild will press the branding concerns Queally described. The California Post said it contacted both the Los Angeles Times and Drop Site News for comment.
news.summary: Nika Soon-Shiong, daughter of LA Times owner Patrick Soon-Shiong, says a sponsored Israeli tourism ad on latimes.com erases Palestinian territories.

news.title: Hermes-toting female 'girlboss' shared video of herself emerging from chauffeured Bentley to 'give back to her community'...but it was all a huge scam, FBI alleges
news.text:
A Hermes-toting Michigan woman flaunted herself as being the picture of success while driving around in a Bentley, but prosecutors claim it was all a phony facade. 

Shannon Monet Steel is accused of duping a number of victims into handing over hundreds of thousands of dollars after giving them false information.

The 42-year-old told one investor she kept her nine-figure fortune in her own private bank and that she was an Ambassador to the Central African Republic.

But federal prosecutors say Steel's wealth was all a lie – and she faces charges of conning investors of over $1 million by falsely portraying herself as a successful businesswoman. 

She was hit with a single count of wire fraud early last month and faces up to 20 years behind bars if convicted, with prosecutors warning that more charges could be on the way.

Since her arrest last month, prosecutors have filed documents in her case revealing what they say is a spending spree in the hopes of convincing a judge to freeze her assets. 

According to prosecutors, the spree ranged from small amounts on groceries, to buying a Bentley Continental, leasing a Maserati and globetrotting.

That same white Bentley was later featured in a Facebook video of her jumping out of it clutching an orange Hermes bag, worth $12,800, while speaking to a group of young girls at a nonprofit for inner city children.

Alongside their motion, they added images captured of Steel behind the wheel of the vehicle while under FBI surveillance and the Maserati inside her rental home, for which she spent $56,000 on renting, wire transfers show. 

Prosecutors said she also bought plane tickets to Paris and Los Angeles late last year as part of her expenditure as they asked the judge to agree to the motion. 

The request said: 'Shannon Steel has defrauded numerous victims out of at least $1.05 million.

'She is now using victim assets to pay her credit card and rent - funds that could otherwise be forfeited and used for restitution.

'Steel has fooled at least eight victims with the lure of millions of dollars in loans, before pocketing the good faith escrow funds of her victims.' 

In the hopes of having the motion agreed to, prosecutors added her American Express statements to their motion.

Those statements detailed her spending in the months leading up to her arrest last month. 

Over the course of three weeks in November and December last year she splashed out $3,500 on flights to Los Angeles and Paris. 

She also spent $752 on Lyft taxis, $195 on having her nails done, and $420 on numerous trips to a spa facility near her home in Farmington Hills, Michigan. 

Other costs included money on takeout food, $3,000 being paid to a law firm and several tabs at a speakeasy in Michigan. 

Prosecutors have already obtained an injunction which saw three of her assets being frozen, including the Bentley and Maserati. 

That injunction also saw that three dozen companies linked to her, her bank accounts, some of her jewelry and other items were also frozen. 

Papers filed for the freeze of her assets pointed to the potential of further charges being brought against her. 

Prosecutors said the alleged scheme also amounted to concealment of money laundering and engaging in transactions related to criminally derived property. Additional charges have yet to be filed against her relating to those allegations. 

The complaint against Steel claimed she used a phony letter from Deutsche Bank to claim that she held an account with around $350 million in it to swindle money from a California-based entrepreneur.

Investigators at Deutsche probed the letter and later told investigators that it was a fake, the complaint said.

Prosecutors allege in the criminal complaint that it was part of a scheme by Steel to present herself as being credible.

Another alleged victim of hers in Ohio handed over $250,000 last November as part of the process to get a $5.4 million loan from her bank, which they never got. 

That same month, another investor trying to buy and renovate a commercial space in Texas handed over $350,000 to secure a $5 million loan, prosecutors said. 

Again, it is alleged that the individual never received the loan. 

As part of the latest motion, investigators said that after getting the money Steel wired $18,100 to her personal savings account at American Express, which she then used to fund her lifestyle. 

The original complaint also painted Steel as being a serial fabricator who used her social media and YouTube to falsely give the impression of being a successful businesswoman. 

Such lies, the complaint claimed, saw her managing to be given a Lifetime President Achievement Award by President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris. 

That award was set up to honor Americans who dedicated over 4,000 hours of volunteering. Steel is said to have lied about completing those volunteer hours to further enhance her image. 

Records seen by the Daily Mail indicate that Steel has a history of bankruptcy and unemployment. 

In 2014 she filed for bankruptcy saying that she was unemployed, had a small amount of money in her checking account and was due over $18,800 to creditors.

She also currently lives at home with her mother in a comfortable but modest $500,000 home in a quiet suburb, that sits close to a McDonald's, according to public records.

And while Steel's own website painted her as an Ambassador to the Central African Republic, federal prosecutors said she was never a diplomat. 

Images posted on her site include images of her with former Namibian President Hage Geingob, it is unclear when these pictures were taken.

The complaint highlighted a series of posts to her Facebook and Instagram page, which have since been deleted, in which she addressed herself as Ambassador Steel.

Quoting her posts, the complaint said she had posted on Instagram saying: 'I was just sworn in as Ambassador for Central African Republic to the United States.'

A post to her Facebook page continued the charade, the complaint claimed, saying she posted: 'I put a whole country on my back #AMBASSADOR STEEL.'

Despite her claims, the complaint said: 'Records with the US Department of State's Office of Foreign Missions indicate that [Steel] is not an accredited diplomat. 

'Nor is she an employee of the United States Government in any capacity as an Ambassador or diplomat to any other country.'

Her website and social media pages also pointed to her owning 'Steel Private Bank', but the complaint said that such a company was never registered with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC). 

Her attorney was approached for comment.
news.summary: Shannon Monet Steel is accused of duping a number of victims into handing over hundreds of thousands of dollars after giving them false information.

news.title: The Cost of Trump Derangement Syndrome
news.text:
He lost 40 percent of his net worth.

Scott Galloway sold all his stocks in a hissy fit when Trump won in 2016 (a taxable event) and then bought back in higher after watching everyone get rich as the market ripped. He lost 40% of his liquid net worth.I told you, this guy's profanely dumb. pic.twitter.com/pvTmSZMTg4— Spencer Pratt (@spencerpratt) September 29, 2026

"Probably my biggest investment mistake was the emotional reaction I had to the 2016 election of Donald Trump," Galloway said. "When he was elected in 2016, I sold all my stocks. That was stupid. The market ripped for the next year."

"There was so much insecurity about him actually winning that the fear had been priced in, stocks ripped up. But what we had from me was an emotional decision and I sold everything," he continued. "I had at that point, a lot of capital gains. So immediately I lost ... so I lost probably a third of the gains to taxes, and then six months later I ended up buying back in on a market that was 10 or 20 percent more expensive. So you could argue, at least notionally, that decision cost me 40 percent of my liquid net worth in stocks."

Boy, that sure taught President Trump a lesson, didn't it?

Remember, Galloway is also the galaxy-brain who wants to see Kamala Harris on the Supreme Court instead of in the White House.

Maybe it's a good idea not to listen to this man on anything, as he admits he makes his decisions based on emotion and not logic, reason, or fact.

I have lived long enough to know that hinging your entire personality and life on your politics is a bad idea. In the last decade or so, we've increasingly seen the Left not just turn politics into a lifestyle, but an all-consuming force that drives them not only to hurt others — see my earlier story about the lawfare waged against conservative lawyers — but also to hurt themselves and even their children, as Nikole Hannah-Jones admitted to doing with her daughter recently.

Political rage is not a good way to live your life, and it's certainly not a good investment strategy. But it should be a lesson to us all that if the Left is willing to harm their children and lose 40 percent of their wealth over politics, maybe they don't have our best interests at heart.

news.title: Troy Jackson Apologizes for ‘Genocide’ Remarks—Where Other Democrats Stand
news.text: Troy Jackson, the Democratic candidate in the Maine Senate race, apologized for recent remarks about how Jewish people view the term “genocide” amid the war in Gaza. Jackson’s recent comments come as Israel remains a major dividing line between him and Republican Senator Susan Collins. The Maine Senate race is expected to be one of the most competitive races of the 2026 midterm elections, and polls point to a close race. Although Maine generally has a Democratic lean, Collins has won by large margins in the past due to her personal popularity and moderate image. Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate, is hoping to dislodge her support among independents and moderate Democrats to flip the seat in the November 3 election, as President Donald Trump’s declining approval rating fuels a more favorable national environment. What to Know Jackson, who has said the United States should not be providing a “blank check” to the Israeli government, has faced scrutiny over the recent remarks made to News Center Maine about how Jewish Americans view the term “genocide.” “It’s unfortunate that there are people here in Maine that don’t like to use that term only because they’re Jewish and what that means to them, with the Holocaust. It fits that description. And it’s an unbelievable thing that’s happened there that people that are innocent are being murdered, and it is a genocide,” he said. Jackson apologized for the remarks in a statement provided to Newsweek on Thursday. “I believe what’s happening in Gaza is genocide, and I also understand that word carries particular weight for many Jewish families given the Holocaust—the genocide of six million Jews,” he said. “In trying to acknowledge that, I misspoke and made a generalization about Jewish Mainers’ views that doesn't reflect what I meant to say.” He said that he apologizes for “the pain that caused.” “Mainers hold a range of deeply considered views, and I promise I will always listen and work to approach these conversations with the care and respect they deserve. In the U.S. Senate, I’ll fight antisemitism and work for lasting peace and security for Palestinians and Israelis,” Jackson said. The “genocide” label remains a divisive sticking point among Democrats. Many more progressive Democrats like Jackson have accused the Israeli government of engaging in a genocide in Gaza, but others have pushed back on that label, arguing that Israel’s actions were in response to an October 7, 2023 attack by Hamas that killed about 1,200 people. At least 74,000 people have died in Gaza, according to the Associated Press, citing Gaza’s Health Ministry. Thirty-one percent of Americans believe Israel’s actions in Gaza constitute a genocide, compared to 20 percent who say Israel has not committed a genocide, according to an AP-NORC poll of 3,040 adults from June 11 to 17, 2026. Troy Jackson vs. Susan Collins: What Latest Polls Say Collins and Jackson are facing a tight race in Maine, according to the latest polling data. Jackson led a new poll of the Senate races from AARP published on Thursday. He was up 3 points, 50 percent to 47 percent, in that poll, which surveyed 982 likely voters from September 20 to 22. It was conducted by Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research. A new co/efficient poll published on Wednesday found that 48 percent of Mainers are planning to vote for Collins, compared to 46 percent who plan to cast their ballot for Jackson. Six percent were undecided. It surveyed 1,240 likely voters from September 28 to 30, 2026, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.77 percentage points. Collins held a 3-point lead in the latest poll from The New York Times, Siena University and The Portland Press Herald released last week, with 49 percent of respondents supporting her reelection bid compared to 46 percent planning to vote for Jackson. It surveyed 619 likely voters from September 15 to 22. However, Jackson had a 4-point lead in a University of New Hampshire poll released the same day. He had support from 51 percent of respondents to Collins’ 47 percent, up from July, when he led by 3 points. It surveyed 1,312 likely voters from September 17 to 21 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.7 percentage points. Where Troy Jackson and Susan Collins Stand on the Israel-Gaza War Jackson has cast himself as a critic of Israel and supports restricting aid to the nation amid its actions in Gaza. Collins is more supportive of Israel and has not used the term “genocide” to describe its actions. “I remain a very strong supporter of Israel, the one democracy in the Middle East. Our true ally in the Middle East, and I think this sadly reflects a rising antisemitism in our country that Graham Platner certainly is part of, and has been since his high school days,” she said in a Fox News interview earlier this year, referring to her original opponent who dropped out amid sexual assault allegations, which he has denied. Why the Maine Senate Race Matters in the 2026 Midterms The Maine Senate race is viewed as a must-win for Democrats hoping to flip control of the chamber, where Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority. Democrats must flip four seats to win a majority, as Vice President JD Vance would serve as the tiebreaker in an evenly split Senate. Given that Maine voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris by 7 points in 2024, the state is a top target for Democrats in an environment that is expected to more heavily favor them. Collins winning reelection would make it more difficult for Democrats to take control of the Senate. It means they would have to win another seat in a more conservative state that backed Trump by double digits in 2024 to stand a chance of winning a majority. Where Other Senate Democratic Candidates Stand on Israel, Gaza Democratic candidates have taken diverging views on Israel ahead of the midterms. Sherrod Brown Brown, a former Senator running to make a comeback in Ohio, has been supportive of Israel in the past. After the October 7 attack, he wrote in a statement that Israel “has the right to exist and the right to self-defense” and that he would “keep working in a bipartisan way to ensure that Israel has the resources to defend itself and that the United States is doing everything we can to support our ally.” Jewish Insider has described him as a “pro-Israel progressive.” Abdul El-Sayed El-Sayed, who is running in Michigan, has been a vocal critic of Israel and has described its conduct in Gaza as a genocide. In a July interview with CNN, he described Israel as a “rogue state” that “did a genocide.” “I would consider them a rogue state. It's a state, and it deserves to be treated in accordance with how it violates human rights and international law. And we are definitely not doing that right now,” he said. He said during a recent interview on the Raging Moderates podcast that he understands his use of the word “genocide” can “pique a lot of really uncomfortable traumas for folks.” “But I’ve also studied my history. When you look at the world’s greatest, worst genocide in history, the greatest crime committed on people that is in memorable history, the murder of 6 million Jews in the Holocaust, coming out of that horrific crime, the word genocide was created to explain what that was,” he said. “The whole point of creating that word is not that you have to wait until the crime is that big again to be able to use it. Otherwise it loses its power.” Mary Peltola Peltola, a former representative who is running for Senate in Alaska, established a more pro-Israel voting record in the House of Representatives. She has not referred to its actions in Gaza as a “genocide.” Her campaign has not focused on foreign policy as she challenges Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican. James Talarico Talarico is running against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in Texas. He has walked a fine line, wanting to bring peace to the region. He has criticized the Israeli government and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu but has also stopped short of using “genocide” to describe its actions. His campaign website states that his “north star” is to “protect innocent life.” “October 7th was the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust — and Israel has the right to defend its people. But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu does not have the right to bomb civilians, restrict aid, or use forced famine and collective punishment as tactics,” his website reads. Josh Turek In Iowa’s Senate race, Turek has described Israel as “one of the few functioning democracies in the Mid East,” but has said that there should not be any “unnecessary killing of civilians and children.” “My thought is that there should be no taxpayer dollars going to any organization, group, regime that is not abiding by international law,” he said in an interview with Iowa Starting Line. news.summary: While Jackson has said Israel conducted a "genocide" in Gaza, other Democratic Senate candidates have taken differing approaches.

news.title: Democrat Optimism in Six Senate Races May Be a Mirage—What the Polls Reveal
news.text: Democrats are optimistic about their chances of flipping the Senate in the midterm elections following a string of favorable polls. But history offers a warning to Democrats, as polls in recent elections underestimated Republicans in key states. Control of the Senate could come down to just a handful of races where polls show razor-thin margins. Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas have emerged as the most competitive races where both parties are hopeful about their chances. Recent polling points to tight races in each of those states. But Republicans have outperformed polling averages in many of those same states over the past few elections. Polling errors are not necessarily repeated from cycle to cycle. But a similar pro-Republican polling error this cycle would not bode well for Democrats’ chances of flipping the Senate. It’s “impossible to know for sure” what the polling error could look like this year, Grant Davis Reeher, professor of political science at Syracuse University, told Newsweek. “There are some pretty big known unknowns in this election, which could throw off polls,” he said. “A primary one is turnout. Polls must make educated guesses about who is most likely to vote. It’s a little trickier in midterms.” This year, there appears to be a motivation gap favoring Democrats, he said. “How much of that has been built into models of likely voters? What if Republicans get some 11th-hour enthusiasm, after those models have been set?” he said. While polls underestimated Republicans in several recent cycles, pollsters adjust their methodologies in response to those misses. That means there is no guarantee that any polling error seen in previous elections will repeat itself in 2026. Why Democrats Are Hopeful About 2026 Midterms Democrats have plenty of reasons to be hopeful about this year’s elections. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat, told Politico in an interview published on Thursday that he’s optimistic about the state of the race. “We have lots of different paths to victory, and we’re not going to turn any of them down,” he told the publication. Historically, when the president is unpopular, his party has suffered losses in the midterms, and President Donald Trump’s approval rating has fallen to record lows in recent polls amid voter frustration with the economy. Trump campaigned on bringing down prices, but the cost of living remains high, and gas prices have soared amid the Iran war. A recent Quinnipiac University poll, for instance, showed that Trump’s net approval stood at -26 points, with 59 percent disapproving and 33 percent approving of the president. That’s the lowest point of the second term and a major warning for Republicans. It surveyed 1,032 registered voters from September 24 to 27, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points. Democrats believe they can exploit his unpopularity to expand the battleground into more conservative states that backed Trump by double digits, like Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas. Doing so is necessary to chip away at Republicans’ 53-47 majority in the November 3 election. Recent special election results have also fueled Democrats’ optimism. Democrats have flipped numerous Republican-held seats in recent special elections. While the low turnout of these races does not necessarily reflect what will be seen in November, they do underscore Democrats’ enthusiasm. These special elections, as well as midterm dynamics and strong polls, have contributed to Democrats’ belief that control of the Senate is competitive this year. Polls Underestimated GOP in Key States in Recent Election Cycles Despite that Democratic optimism, there is still a risk that polls could be underestimating Republicans in several of these key races. CNN data analyst Harry Enten said Wednesday that Republicans outperformed the polls by several points in the three Midwestern states with key Senate races this year—by 9 points in Iowa, 6 points in Ohio and 5 points in Michigan. “I will note that the leads that the Democrats have in all of these races right now are under how much the GOP outperformed back in 2024,” he said. “So you look at this, and you go, you know what, maybe we should just hold on a second here because we've seen this dance before. And it was not a dance that Democrats like when the votes were actually cast and counting.” A similar polling error also played out in 2018, the midterm during Trump’s first term in office when he was not on the ballot, Enten said. What Could Polling Error Mean in Six Key Senate Races? A pro-Republican polling error in the six key Senate races would indicate these races are closer than they appear, or that Republican candidates have an outright advantage to hold onto the Senate majority in the midterms. Alaska Republican Senator Dan Sullivan is facing a challenge from Democratic former Representative Mary Peltola, in what has become one of the most closely watched races of the midterms. The latest polls do show a tight race between the two candidates. The latest Alaska Survey Research poll showed Peltola up 4 points, 52 percent to 48 percent, while a recent AARP poll showed Peltola up 6 points, 53 percent to 47 percent. The Alaska Survey Research poll surveyed 1,352 likely voters from September 10 to 12, while the AARP poll surveyed 800 likely voters from September 8 to 11. But those polls have been off in the state before. In 2020, an Alaska Survey Research poll showed Sullivan up 4 points, according to Alaska Public Media. He ended up winning by nearly 13. In 2022, the AARP poll showed Republicans Lisa Murkowski and Kelly Tshibaka tied on the final ballot of ranked-choice, but Murkowski won by more than 7 points. Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sullivan, emphasized that the state is tough to poll in a statement to Newsweek on Thursday. "Alaska is a notoriously difficult state to poll – even local outfits like Alaska Survey Research are perennially wrong, despite trying really, really hard,” Adams said. “With the election a month away, our campaign is confident about where things currently stand and where they are heading." Newsweek reached out to the Peltola campaign for comment via email. Iowa Polls in Iowa are close. RealClearPolitics’ polling aggregate showed Democratic state Representative Josh Turek with a 0.3 point lead over Republican U.S. Representative Ashley Hinson. That means that even a slight polling error benefiting Hinson would shift the race. Polls underestimated Trump in 2024. The final polling average from 270toWin showed Trump up 4.7 points, 50 percent to 45.3 percent, but Trump ended up carrying the state by 13 points. A recent poll from Quantus Insights showed Hinson up slightly, 47.1 percent to 45.8 percent, while an InsiderAdvantage poll gave Turek a slight advantage, 47.4 percent to 45.7 percent. The Quantus poll surveyed 738 Iowans from September 28 to 29 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points, while the survey from InsiderAdvantage was conducted among 1,200 likely voters from September 22 to 23, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. Newsweek reached out to the Hinson and Turek campaigns for comment via email. Maine In Maine, Republican Senator Susan Collins is facing a challenge from Democrat Troy Jackson, the former Maine Senate president. Although Maine leans toward Democrats, Collins has won in the past due to her personal popularity and bipartisan image. That includes 2020, when polls consistently showed her trailing her Democratic challenger Sara Gideon. Newsweek reached out to the Collins and Jackson campaigns for comment via email. Gideon was up 3.8 points in 270toWin’s polling average, but Collins went on to win with nearly 51 percent of the vote, while Gideon received less than 43 percent. A progressive independent candidate received nearly 5 percent of the vote, which is notable because Maine uses ranked-choice voting. Had Collins fallen below 50 percent, those voters may have been more aligned with Gideon, though it’s not clear exactly how that would have broken down. It was still a large polling miss that looms over this year’s race. Jackson led a new poll of the Senate races from AARP published on Thursday. He was up 3 points, 50 percent to 47 percent. However, a poll from The New York Times showed Collins up 3 points, 49 percent to 46 percent. The AARP poll surveyed 982 likely voters from September 20 to 22 and was conducted by Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research. The Times poll surveyed 619 likely voters from September 15 to 22. Michigan Senator Gary Peters, a Democrat, is retiring in Michigan, leaving a seat open in one of the country's most competitive battlegrounds. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers are competing to succeed him. Michigan backed Trump by about 1.4 points in 2024. Polls were slightly off, with former Vice President Kamala Harris leading by 1.8 points in 270toWin’s aggregate. El-Sayed held a 3.4-point lead in RealClearPolitics’ polling average on Thursday. The latest Fox News poll showed El-Sayed up a single point, 50 percent to 49 percent, while a Marist University survey showed him up 7 points, 51 percent to 44 percent. The Fox News poll, conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research, surveyed 1,028 likely voters from September 24 to 28 with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. The Marist poll surveyed 1,235 registered voters from September 24 to 27, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points. Newsweek reached out to the El-Sayed and Rogers campaigns for comment via email. Ohio Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown is seeking a comeback in Ohio, a one-time battleground state that shifted rightward over the past decade. Polls suggest a close race against Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill the seat vacated by Vice President JD Vance. Brown was up 3.7 points in RCP’s aggregate as of Thursday. A recent Suffolk University poll showed him up 3 points, 47 percent to 44 percent, while he led by 8 points, 51 percent to 43 percent, in a Marist University poll. The Suffolk poll surveyed 500 likely voters from September 23 to 27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points, while the Marist poll was conducted from September 24 to 27 among 1,298 registered voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points. But like other key states, Republicans were underestimated in Ohio in the most recent cycle. Trump was up 7.7 points in 270toWin’s average, but went on to win by just over 11 points in November. Newsweek reached out to the Brown and Husted campaigns for comment via email. Texas The GOP stronghold of Texas has emerged as part of the battleground this year, as Democratic state Representative James Talarico and Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton face off in an increasingly close race, according to the polls. A Big Data Poll gave Talarico a 2-point lead, 47 percent to 45 percent, while a survey from Barbara Jordan Public Policy Research at Texas Southern University and Survey Center showed Talarico up 1 point, 47 percent to 46 percent. Overall, Talarico was up 2.7 points in RCP’s average. The Big Data Poll surveyed 698 likely voters from September 24 to 26, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. Meanwhile, the poll from TSU was conducted from September 15 to 19 among 1,800 likely voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.31 percentage points. In 2024, Trump held an average lead of 7.4 percentage points in polls, according to the 270toWin aggregate. But he went on to win by nearly 14 points. Newsweek reached out to the Paxton and Talarico campaigns for comment via email. What Happens Next Polls will continue to be watched as a key gauge of where the electorate stands over the coming weeks as the midterms approach. Candidates are making their cases to voters in these key swing states in hopes of motivating their base to turn out to the polls, as well as to win over undecided voters. Issues including Trump’s approval rating, the economy and war in Iran could shape voter behavior in the final weeks of campaign season. news.summary: Democrats are optimistic about their chances of flipping the Senate, but polls have overestimated them in the past.

news.title: Donald Trump approval ratings fall to alarming level ahead of November 2026 US midterm elections: Only 17 per cent of American adults now approve Republican President
news.text:
APPresident Donald Trump speaks with reporters before boarding Marine One on the South Lawn of the White House. (AP Photo)

Donald Trump's approval ratings among Americans on the President's handling of the price rise and overall economy has witnessed jaw-dropping drop.
